## Shipping baseline: what the repository enforces today

### S1: Done (verified); severity none; stage n/a; effort none

**Plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Every change ships with tests. The full suite, browser tests and all CI jobs stay green. Add new CI jobs where this prompt asks.'

**Current state.** The CI definitions are mechanical and broad (this item covers what the workflows run; whether a red job blocks a merge is S1.required, and the gaps are S1.gaps). ci.yml runs on every pull request and on push to main: 15 jobs, 17 checks with the 3-Python matrix. test (py 3.11/3.12/3.13, Postgres 16 service so the Postgres variants run: uv sync --locked, ruff check, ruff format --check, mypy src tests, pytest, doc snippets, `mendari test` on 5 packs); browser (pytest -m browser, Chromium); reference-pack; r4-structure; fhir-conformance (HL7 validator 6.10.4, US Core 6.1.0, Da Vinci IGs); sandbox-e2e (docker compose: HAPI, SMART launcher, two engines); hub-site (Next.js lint, typecheck, build, Playwright); hub-e2e (sdist and wheel, check_sdist, clean-venv install); cql; security (pip-audit, npm audit, OWASP ZAP); secrets (gitleaks, full history); docs (mkdocs build --strict); quickstart; pilot-check; docker. packs.yml runs on pull requests touching packs/** (validate, test, card, eval, regression gate against the base benchmark). release.yml and images.yml run only on v* tags (environments pypi and ghcr). neon-preview-cleanup.yml runs when a pull request closes. Lint: ruff E,F,W,I,B,UP,SIM,RUF minus RUF012. Types: mypy with check_untyped_defs and warn_unused_ignores, not strict, ignore_missing_imports on. Pytest turns warnings into errors. Workflow hygiene is itself tested (actions pinned to commits, read-only tokens, no fork-context triggers, images pinned by digest). I re-ran lint, format and types exactly as CI does: all pass.

### S1.gaps: Partial (verified); severity medium; stage 3; effort M (1-3 days)

**Plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Every change ships with tests. The full suite, browser tests and all CI jobs stay green.'

**Current state.** Gaps between the rule and what is enforced. (1) Nothing checks that a change ships with tests: no coverage tool in the dev group, no coverage gate, only a pull-request checkbox. (2) The suite has 2,264 collected tests; the default selection is 2,121 (143 deselected: 142 browser, 1 slow). The orchestrator's default run: 1,848 passed, 273 skipped, 201.93 s (the per-test times in its junit file sum to 198 s; I did not re-run the whole suite). Of the 273 skips, 270 are Postgres-only (267 parametrised variants and 3 Postgres-only tests), which run only when MENDARI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set, and 3 need HL7 files cached under var/. So a local green run is not CI's green run. CLAUDE.md still says the full suite takes '< 3 s'; collection alone takes about 3.5 s. (3) Tests that pytest runs in no workflow: the `slow` structural R4 gate over HL7's 5,309 examples, two tests that skip unless hl7.fhir.r4.core is cached, and one that skips unless HL7's schema zip is cached (that last check does run in CI another way: the r4-structure job runs the generator and diffs the result). (4) Collecting the suite creates var/mendari.db in the working directory, because tests/test_vercel.py imports mendari.server.vercel, which builds the app at import with a relative SQLite path. I reproduced this in a scratch directory: an empty directory had var/mendari.db (192,512 bytes) after `pytest --co`. (5) No scheduled workflow exists. Dependabot is configured (monthly, five ecosystems), so dependency pull requests do re-run CI each month, but pip-audit, npm audit and gitleaks run only when someone pushes; Dependabot security updates are a repository setting the owner must turn on (not visible in the repository).

### S2: Done (verified); severity none; stage n/a; effort none

**Plan says.** not in plan (the shared header on p.6 has no rule about regenerating derived pack artifacts; only CLAUDE.md has it). Nearest principle, p.2: 'Every build uses real deterministic computation'.

**Current state.** Enforced by CI job reference-pack: it runs scripts/build-reference-pack.sh (synthetic data -> trained model -> pack tests -> benchmark -> card, five packs) and fails if any tracked file under packs/ or datasets/ differs, except evals/benchmark.json and DECISION_CARD.md, which are excluded (see S10). Generators use fixed seeds; naive Bayes training and temperature fitting use no randomness. I regenerated, in scratch copies, the train/calibration/test splits of all five packs, both trained models (inbox and referral) and all five local-site datasets, on macOS with Python 3.12.12: every file is byte-identical to the committed one (the auditor had checked the inbox pack only), so reproducibility also holds off CI's Ubuntu. Pack identity is a content digest. Limits. (a) Ten committed data files, two per pack (290 records: red_flags, exclusions, urgent_referrals, documentation_notes, unsafe_drafts and their holdouts), are hand-written, not generated: `mendari sandbox generate` does not write them, so they are source, covered by the pack digest but by no reproducibility or provenance check. (b) The script names the five packs by hand; no test ties its list to the packs/ directory. (c) `git diff --exit-code` ignores untracked files, so a generator that began writing a new file would not fail the job. (d) CI checks one platform (ubuntu, Python 3.12).

### S4: Missing (verified); severity high; stage 3; effort M (1-3 days)

**Plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Every computation and statistic is real and deterministic (seeded where random).' p.3 lists 'confidence intervals' as blocking grading credibility.

**Current state.** No function in src/ computes a confidence interval, a hypothesis test or a resample (the only statistics import is statistics.fmean for mean latency). What exists is point estimates and fixed thresholds: metrics.classification (accuracy, per-label precision/recall/F1, macro-F1, confusion); metrics.calibration (ECE over equal-width bins); metrics.brier; metrics.percentiles (mean, p50, p95, max); metrics.threshold_sweep; metrics.rates; harness.build_report (critical detection rate, false automation rate and share, expected override rate, recommendation accuracy, subgroups); compare.compare (flags a drop > 2 x tolerance; minimum sizes MIN_GROUP=15, MIN_LABEL_SUPPORT=10); gate.gate (tolerance, and EPSILON=1e-9 on critical detection); monitoring._psi (alert at 0.25; minimum counts 20/50/20); share.shareable (drops cells under 10); agreement.agreement (exact match); calibration.fit_temperature (grid search). None takes a seed because none is random; randomness exists only in the sandbox generators (fixed seeds 7/11, 17/23, 29/31, 37/41, 43/47) and one shuffle with Random(0). So no reported metric has an interval: accuracy, macro-F1, per-label figures, ECE, Brier, outcome rates, false automation, critical detection, subgroups, leaderboard rows (ranked by point accuracy), monitoring's observed accuracy and override rate, and site-shared summaries. The committed benchmarks show why it matters: trial note_pancreatitis is 6/6 (Wilson 95% lower bound 0.61), note_pregnancy 12/13 (0.667), inbox urgent 23/23 (0.857), prior-auth red_flag 25/25 (0.867); ai-guard unsafe_advice is 102/164 (lower bound 0.546).

### S5: Partial (verified); severity medium; stage 3; effort M (1-3 days)

**Plan says.** Principle, p.2: 'Model-agnostic.'

**Current state.** The interface is vendor-neutral: Provider is an ABC with one abstract method, answer(inputs) -> ProviderOutput (a probability distribution per question), plus optional preflight, batching and budget hooks. Any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint works through the single `llm` type by setting LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY and LLM_MODEL (a test covers a local server and a remote https endpoint); no shipped pack pins a model. In practice the committed leaderboards hold rows for three LLMs from two vendors (anthropic/claude-sonnet-5, anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5, openai/gpt-oss-120b) and for Jev. But a vendor whose API is not OpenAI-compatible needs code changes in several places, because the registry is a fixed dict with no plug-in mechanism and provider types are hard-coded outside providers/: daily budgets and organization quotas (jev, llm), the deployment-variable deny list, health output and a Jev-only route, `mendari calibrate` (llm only), `mendari train` (naive_bayes only) and the leaderboard label. The llm request body also carries gateway-specific fields (a `reasoning.effort` object; cost read from `usage.cost`), and there is one LLM endpoint per deployment (LLM_BASE_URL is global).

### S6: Done (verified); severity none; stage n/a; effort none

**Plan says.** not in plan (neither the shared header on p.6 nor the principles on p.2 mention the audit chain).

**Current state.** The mechanism works and is tested (SQLite locally; the same tests run on Postgres in CI). Append: _append/_append_many read the last event's hash (GENESIS = 64 zeros at the start), compute sha256 over prev, decision id, event name, canonical JSON payload and timestamp joined by 0x1f, and insert under an exclusive session (a Postgres advisory lock serialises appends). Verify: verify() recomputes every event hash in seq order and, for decision.created, the sha256 of the stored decision record; with --notes it also checks each kept note against the commitment its event chained. Fifteen event types: decision.created, review.resolved, outcome.recorded, feedback.recorded, pas.submitted, input.read, input.purged, note.erased, governance.approved, governance.revoked, deployment.recorded, key.created, key.revoked, client.registered, client.revoked. Exposed as GET /api/audit/verify and `mendari audit verify [--notes]`. What verify() does not cover is S6.coverage.

**Evidence.**

- src/mendari/core/audit.py:41 - GENESIS; :48 - _CHAIN_LOCK; :720-775 - _append/_append_many (reads the head at :733-734, inserts prev_hash and hash)

- src/mendari/core/audit.py:1816-1845 - verify(): chain recomputed; record_sha256 checked for decision.created; returns the head
- src/mendari/core/audit.py:405, 466, 501, 522, 596, 854, 873, 997, 1028, 1329, 1347, 1412, 1507, 1541, 1592, 1636 - every _append call; src/mendari/server/app.py:1181-1183 - record_event(..., 'pas.submitted')

- tests/test_audit.py::test_hash_chain_detects_tampering; ::test_hash_chain_detects_deleted_events

### S6.coverage: Partial (verified); severity high; stage 4; effort L (1-2 weeks)

**Plan says.** not in plan. Nearest principle, p.2: 'Grades are scoped and versioned', and the vision's 'trusted'.

**Current state.** State-changing routes and commands. CHAINED: POST /api/packs/{ns}/{name}/decide, .../guard, .../fhir/decide, POST /fhir/$decide, POST /cds-services/{id}, POST /api/smart/decide (decision.created through Decision.decide -> store.record); POST /api/review/{id} (review.resolved); POST /api/audit/{id}/outcome (outcome.recorded); POST /api/audit/{id}/feedback (feedback.recorded); POST .../pas with submit (pas.submitted); POST and DELETE /api/governance (governance.approved/revoked); POST and DELETE /api/auth/keys (key.created/revoked); POST and DELETE /api/auth/clients (client.registered/revoked); a reader's read of a kept input or note (input.read); server start when a pack or provider deployment changes (deployment.recorded); CLI `mendari decide --db`, `mendari phi purge` (input.purged, note.erased), `mendari notes erase` (note.erased). READ-ONLY POSTs: /fhir/Questionnaire/$questionnaire-package and /fhir/{resource}/_search. NOT CHAINED: POST /api/packs/{ns}/{name}/evals and `mendari eval --db` (an eval_reports row; a security-log line only); sign-in, sign-out and SMART launch sessions; POST of the token endpoint (access tokens and jti claims); provider, organization and rate-limit counters; capability_versions (deliberately outside the chain lock); startup migrations; the derived queue columns on decisions (review_status, final_label); and the WHOLE registry service (create namespace, PATCH publisher type i.e. verification, issue token, add key, publish a pack version, add a site report), which has its own database and no chain. No test enumerates state-changing routes and asserts each is classified, so a new route can skip the chain silently. verify() also has blind spots, all reproduced in scratch databases: (1) an edited stored evaluation report (accuracy 0.75 changed to 0.5) still verifies; (2) an edited decisions.final_label still verifies; (3) deleting the last two events plus that decision row still verifies (ok true, events 2); (4) verify() does not reconcile the side tables with the chain: after a governance approval was revoked, setting revoked_at back to NULL in the table made active_approval() return it again, and an approval row inserted with no chained event was also treated as active, with verify() ok both times. That last one is a safety lever: an approval is what lets a risk level 2-3 pack automate. Nothing anchors the chain head outside the database. All four need write access to the database.

### S7: Partial (verified); severity blocker; stage 2; effort S (<1 day)

**Plan says.** Principle, p.2: 'Synthetic-only sandbox.' p.3 (today): hosted inputs 'stored in plaintext, can't be erased'.

**Current state.** The PHI modes are real and tested, but the safe ones are opt-in. MENDARI_PHI_MODE: `off` (the default) keeps the input inside the chained decision record when the pack says store_input: full (the spec default, and what all five packs set); `hash` keeps no input and refuses notes; `encrypt` seals inputs, evidence and notes apart from the chain with AES-256-GCM so retention can delete them, and chains every read. hash and encrypt refuse to start without a keyed input-hash key. The hosted entrypoint requires no mode, so a hosted deployment with default settings stores inputs in plaintext in a record that cannot be erased without breaking the chain. That matches the plan's p.3 'today' row and is still true at this commit. The code itself treats `off` as the synthetic-data mode. Only the pilot-check CI job and the on-premises and Kubernetes templates set encrypt. Severity is blocker because this is the hosted-access gate that prompt A5 owns (the A5 unit carries the detail); the test coverage of the modes themselves is good.

**Evidence.**

- src/mendari/core/phi.py:1-11 - the three modes; :138-161 - phi_policy(): default 'off'; hash/encrypt need MENDARI_INPUT_HASH_KEY, encrypt needs MENDARI_PHI_KEY
- src/mendari/core/audit.py:374-376 - keep = store_input == 'full' and mode != 'hash'; in_record = keep and mode == 'off'; record['input'] = dict(inputs) if in_record
- src/mendari/core/spec.py:407-408 - AuditConfig.store_input: Literal['full', 'hash'] = 'full'; $ grep -n store_input packs/*/pack.yaml -> `store_input: full` in all five
- src/mendari/server/vercel.py:55-61 - hosted app built with no PHI-mode requirement; src/mendari/server/app.py:325 - phi = phi_policy() (only a bad setting fails)
- src/mendari/server/security_log.py:39-42 - 'in off mode (synthetic data) the server prints it as before'
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:458 - only the pilot-check job sets MENDARI_PHI_MODE: encrypt; deploy/onprem/.env.example:20 and deploy/kubernetes/mendari.yaml:27 - encrypt
- tests/test_phi.py::test_hash_mode_stores_no_input; ::test_encrypt_mode_keeps_only_ciphertext_and_reveals_it_to_readers; ::test_retention_purges_inputs_and_keeps_the_chain
- tests/test_record_hygiene.py::test_no_lab_value_date_or_patient_id_is_stored; ::test_startup_is_refused_without_the_key; ::test_pilot_check_requires_keyed_hashes
- tests/test_notes.py::test_phi_mode_hash_refuses_a_note_and_keeps_nothing
- $ pytest tests/test_phi.py tests/test_record_hygiene.py tests/test_notes.py (in the 9-file run) -> passed

**Recommendation.** Make the hosted entrypoint refuse to start in PHI mode off unless an explicit synthetic-only setting is given (so the choice is recorded), and default hosted deployments to encrypt or hash. Prompt A5 owns this; the Definition of shipped should name the startup check.

### S7.prod: Partial (inferred); severity medium; stage 2; effort S (<1 day)

**Plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Never touch production or the hosted deployment.'

**Current state.** Convention plus a few guards; no mechanical barrier, and the deployment wiring works against the rule. In tests: every test gets its own Hub config and cache directories and has the registry URL and token removed; provider tests set fake keys and use httpx.MockTransport. There is no socket-blocking guard, so a test or a session with live credentials in its environment could reach hosted services. On deployment: vercel.json disables Git deployments only for dependabot/** branches, and the preview-cleanup workflow says the Neon integration creates a database branch for every preview deployment. If the Vercel project is connected to the repository (a hosted setting I could not check), every branch a build session pushes gets a hosted preview with its own database branch, and every merge to main redeploys production, where startup migrations then run against the production database. So a prompt cannot both merge and 'never touch the hosted deployment'.

### S10: Partial (verified); severity high; stage 3; effort M (1-3 days)

**Plan says.** Principle, p.2: 'Grades are scoped and versioned. Each grade names the pack, dataset and model versions it applies to.'

**Current state.** Regeneration exists; staleness detection does not. What is regenerated: the build script rewrites evals/benchmark.json and DECISION_CARD.md for the five packs with the default local providers. evals/leaderboard.json (the provider comparison, which needs live Jev and LLM credentials) is written only by a manual `mendari leaderboard` run and merges into existing rows. What fails when they are stale: nothing. The reference-pack job explicitly excludes benchmark.json and DECISION_CARD.md from its byte-identical check; no test compares a benchmark's pack digest with the pack's digest; `mendari validate`, `mendari test` and `mendari card` say nothing; the registry shows a shipped benchmark and leaderboard as they are. I changed one policy threshold (auto 0.90 -> 0.91) in a scratch copy of the inbox pack: validate passed, the 16 pack tests passed, the version stayed 0.3.0, and the card printed the new digest next to the old benchmark's figures with no warning. The packs workflow gates a pull request's fresh evaluation against the base benchmark but never requires the committed files to be refreshed. Today the five committed benchmarks and cards are in step (digest equal, card equals a fresh render), by discipline. The leaderboards are not: the trial and prior-auth leaderboards were built at pack version 0.1.0 and the packs are 0.1.2; ai-guard and referral mix rows from two versions; rows carry pack_version but no digest, and the card's table has no version column. The exclusion from CI is avoidable: for all five packs, two evaluations differ only in id, created_at and latency_ms, and a fresh run matches the committed benchmark on every other field.

**Evidence.**

- .github/workflows/ci.yml:79 - `git diff --exit-code -- packs datasets ':!packs/*/evals/benchmark.json' ':!packs/*/DECISION_CARD.md'`

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:199-200 - 'id': uuid4, 'created_at': now; :244 - latency_ms (the non-deterministic fields)
- src/mendari/core/card.py:39-54 - read_benchmark checks shape only, never report['pack']['digest'] against pack.digest; :75 - prints the current digest; :263-268 - prints the benchmark's date
- src/mendari/evals/leaderboard.py:78-98 - build() keeps existing rows whatever their pack_version; :141-164 - markdown() has no version column

- $ python (5 packs): benchmark pack digest == pack digest -> True x5; `mendari card <pack>` == committed DECISION_CARD.md -> True x5
- $ python (leaderboards): clinical-trial-prescreener rows at ['0.1.0'], pack 0.1.2; prior-auth-preflight ['0.1.0'] vs 0.1.2; ai-guard ['0.1.1', '0.1.2']; referral-router ['0.1.0', '0.1.1']; inbox ['0.3.0']; row keys include pack_version, no digest
- $ (scratch copy, policy.yaml auto 0.90 -> 0.91): `mendari validate` -> rc 0 'ok mendari/patient-inbox-router@0.3.0 sha256:886879ed...'; `mendari test` -> 16 passed; `mendari card` -> rc 0, 'Pack digest sha256:886879ed...', 'Last validation 2026-09-30 on test (n=600 ...)', accuracy 99.3%, no stale wording; the benchmark's pack digest is sha256:5e405f48...
- $ (scratch) `mendari eval <pack> --dataset test` twice for each of 5 packs -> differ only at /created_at, /id, /latency_ms/*; run vs committed benchmark -> the same fields only
- .github/workflows/packs.yml:45-54 - evaluates the change and gates against base, but writes to /tmp only

**Recommendation.** Make staleness mechanical: (a) in reference-pack, compare the regenerated benchmark.json with the committed one after dropping id, created_at and latency_ms, and the card after dropping the date and latency lines; (b) have read_benchmark and leaderboard.read refuse, or loudly mark, a report or row whose pack digest differs from the pack's, on the card, the API and the Hub; (c) store pack digest and model id per leaderboard row and show the version column; (d) fail the packs workflow when the digest changes without a version bump and CHANGELOG entry.

### S12: Partial (verified); severity medium; stage 4; effort M (1-3 days)

**Plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Never weaken an existing safety rule, cap or check to make a test pass.' (CLAUDE.md: 'Policy only lowers automation ... Providers never raise anything but ProviderError'.)

**Current state.** The caps are enforced in one place and tested by example. apply_policy runs pack rules first, then thresholds, then _cap, which can only turn AUTO into HUMAN_REVIEW: a label with allow_auto false, any provider failure, an automation_requires slot not running an allowed variant, and the risk level (levels 0-1 may automate; 2-3 only with a recorded governance override; 4 never). Tests in tests/test_policy.py: test_thresholds, test_emergency_rule_wins_over_confident_routing, test_emergency_rule_respects_its_confidence_floor, test_provider_failure_never_automates, test_missing_primary_answer_abstains, test_risk_levels_2_and_3_require_review_unless_governance_allows, test_risk_level_4_is_never_autonomous, test_governance_override_needs_accountability, test_automation_can_require_provider_variants; plus governance and budget tests. Limits. (1) The invariant is checked on hand-picked cases; there is no property or exhaustive test. I ran a seeded sweep of 20,000 random cases (risk level, answers, failures, governance) against the inbox manifest and found no cap violation, so the code holds; the repository just does not prove it. (2) 'Policy only lowers automation' is true of the caps, not of a pack's own policy: at risk level 0 or 1 a pack rule may set outcome AUTO, and a per-label auto_threshold may be lower than the general one, even lower than the review threshold; neither is validated. Confirmed on the inbox manifest: a label threshold of 0.10 automates at confidence 0.55 (general threshold 0.90) and at 0.20 (below the review threshold 0.50); a rule with outcome AUTO automates at confidence 0.20, where the default is ABSTAIN (the caps still apply to it: with a provider failure it becomes HUMAN_REVIEW, and at risk level 2 or above the manifest is refused). That is the pack author's stated policy and it shows on the card, but it matters once packs come from outside authors. (3) ProviderError: remote providers map HTTP, timeout, credential, size and shape failures to stable codes with no remote body, tested per provider; but Decision.decide catches only ProviderError, so any other exception from a provider is a 500 with no decision recorded (nothing automates, yet nothing is audited), and no test sweeps all provider types with hostile input. (4) Nothing marks which tests and constants are safety checks, so 'never weaken' cannot be checked by a reviewer or by CI.

**Evidence.**

- src/mendari/core/policy.py:20-21 - MAX_AUTONOMOUS_RISK = CLINICAL_INFORMATION; OVERRIDABLE_RISK = levels 2-3
- src/mendari/core/spec.py:588-591 - a rule requesting AUTO is refused only at risk level >= 2; :373-375 - LabelPolicy.auto_threshold: 0..1 with no relation to thresholds.auto or thresholds.review; :366-370 - only review <= auto is checked

**Recommendation.** Add a property test (seeded random answers, failures, risk levels and variants) asserting that the outcome with caps is never more automated than without, and that failures never yield AUTO. For packs from outside authors, require auto_threshold >= thresholds.auto and forbid rule outcome AUTO (or cap such packs at HUMAN_REVIEW, as the unaudited community-packs branch plans). In decide(), turn an unexpected provider exception into a recorded failure code so the decision is audited and reviewed instead of a 500; add a sweep test over PROVIDER_TYPES. Mark safety tests with a pytest marker and fail CI when a marked test is deleted or skipped.

## Every plan defect, in full

### D1 (principles)

**The plan says.** All four proprietary parts stay proprietary while every prompt, A8-A11 included, is run 'in the Mendari repository on a new branch from main' (pp.1, 6)

**Why it is wrong.** The plan never says where proprietary code or data lives. Followed literally, the hidden-set workflow, the grading service, the registry and the site network are all built inside the Apache-2.0 repository that is opened at stage 3, next to the registry, Hub and leaderboard code that is already there. The plan's own rationale ('a competitor can copy open code; it cannot copy your hidden test sets, your grading track record or your site relationships') suggests only data, keys and operations need to be private, but that is not stated, and A8 gives no storage location for hidden-set content.

- launch-plan p.1 lines 19-25; p.6 shared header
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py, src/mendari/evals/leaderboard.py, src/mendari/evals/share.py, hub/ - already in the tree; LICENSE:1-3 covers the whole tree
- pyproject.toml:73-78 - registry and leaderboard ship in the wheel

**Proposed correction.** Add a section 'What is private and where it lives': hidden-set content, labels, signing keys and site agreements in a private store or second repository; state explicitly whether the grading and registry code is open. Add to the A8-A11 headers: 'no hidden-set content, key or site identity is ever committed to this repository or its fixtures'.

### D2 (principles)

**The plan says.** A9: within each arm, search the declared provider variants and report the best configuration; rank on the frozen hidden sets (p.17)

**Why it is wrong.** Choosing the best variant per arm on the same cases used to rank the arms is selection on the test set: the reported score of each arm is biased upward, more so for arms with more variants and models (the LLM arm already has six measured configurations per dataset against one or two for Jev and for offline), and the Holm adjustment across the six arm pairs does not account for it.

- $ python (leaderboard rows by arm, per dataset) -> llm 6 configurations on every dataset; jev 1-2; offline 1-2
- launch-plan p.17 lines 575-580; p.18 lines 597-599

**Proposed correction.** Select each arm's configuration on a separate selection split (or the public development sets) and score only the selected configuration on the hidden set; or report every configuration and adjust for all of them. State the rule in the published grading method.

### D3 (principles)

**The plan says.** A grade is published when every critical label has at least 100 positive cases; a difference that is not significant after adjustment is a tie and passes to the next criterion (p.18)

**Why it is wrong.** With 100 positives the top criterion can rarely separate packs. A perfect 100/100 has an exact two-sided 95% lower bound of 96.4%; 95/100 gives 88.7% to 98.4% and 99/100 gives 94.6% to 100%, so recall of 95% and 99% cannot be told apart. With exact McNemar and Holm across six arm pairs the smallest threshold is 0.0083, which needs at least eight discordant positives all in one direction (0 against 8 gives p = 0.0078; 0 against 6 gives 0.031), so on 100 positives two arms must differ by about eight detected emergencies before the scoreboard may rank them. Nearly every comparison on critical-label recall will therefore be a 'tie', and the ranking will in practice be decided by accuracy and cost, the opposite of the stated priority. Treating non-significance as equivalence also rewards small test sets.

- $ python (exact Clopper-Pearson by bisection on the binomial tail) -> 100/100: 0.9638-1; 95/100: 0.8872-0.9836; 99/100: 0.9455-0.9997; 60/60: 0.9404-1; 72/72: 0.9501-1; 150/152: 0.9533-0.9984; smallest n with n/n lower bound of 0.95 or more: 72; with one miss 110; with two misses 142
- $ python (exact two-sided McNemar on discordant pairs) -> (0, 4): 0.125; (0, 6): 0.031; (1, 7): 0.070; (0, 8): 0.0078; Holm's first threshold for six pairs: 0.0083
- launch-plan p.18 lines 597-611
- $ python (critical n in each committed benchmark) -> largest today: referral 113 and 124, ai-guard 164, 114, 164 and 62; inbox 23, prior-auth 25, trial 6-29

**Proposed correction.** Publish the interval beside every grade and set a minimum lower bound for critical-label recall as a pass/fail floor before any ranking (a lower bound of at least 95% needs 72 of 72, 109 of 110 or 140 of 142). Use an equivalence margin, not non-significance, to declare ties, and size the hidden sets from that margin.

### D4 (principles)

**The plan says.** A9 ranking criterion 1 is 'critical-label recall', reported per critical label, with Holm adjustment 'across the pairs of arms' (pp.17-18)

**Why it is wrong.** For a pack with several critical labels the first criterion is a vector, and the plan does not say how a vector is ranked (worst label, all labels, a fixed order) or that the adjustment must cover labels as well as arm pairs. The trial pack has six critical labels and AI Guard four, so six arm pairs become 24 to 36 comparisons on criterion 1 alone, and two arms can each win on a different label.

- $ python (critical items in each committed benchmark) -> trial 6 critical labels, ai-guard 4, referral 2, inbox 1, prior-auth 1
- src/mendari/dashboard/leaderboard.js:14 - the dashboard already had to choose a rule (the minimum detection rate over critical labels)
- launch-plan p.17 line 582; p.18 lines 597-608

**Proposed correction.** Define criterion 1 as the lowest critical-label recall (or its lowest interval bound) and state that the Holm family is every label by arm-pair comparison made for that criterion.

### D5 (principles)

**The plan says.** Model-agnostic; Mendari has no preferred model provider; and every pack is scored as Mendari alone, + Jev, + LLM, + Jev + LLM (p.2)

**Why it is wrong.** The four arms themselves privilege one vendor: Jev, a single company's product, defines two of the four arms by name, while every other model vendor is folded into one 'LLM' arm. 'LLM' is also not one thing: the committed comparisons already show three models with different results. The plan acknowledges the relationship elsewhere (conflict-of-interest policy naming TypeSafe, p.13) but not in the principle.

- launch-plan p.2 lines 40-41; p.13 lines 399-400
- $ python (models in leaderboard rows) -> jev-1.13.0, anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5, anthropic/claude-sonnet-5, openai/gpt-oss-120b

**Proposed correction.** Define arms by provider class ('+ typed classifier', '+ general LLM', '+ both') with each named model as an entry within its class, Jev being the first typed classifier; or keep the Jev arms and print the disclosure on every scoreboard. Require the model id on every arm label.

### D6 (principles)

**The plan says.** Every pack is scored in four configurations (p.2)

**Why it is wrong.** Not every pack can have four arms. A pack whose questions are all structured (criteria, CQL, dosing) has only the first. The repository's own decision of 2026-10-04 restricts community packs to local providers, so they would have one arm by rule. Three of the five reference packs cannot express Jev + LLM today because they have one remote slot and no combined variant.

- tasks/todo.md:8-10 - community packs 'recommend only (never AUTO, local providers only)'
- $ python (pack.yaml variants) -> no variant in any pack combines jev and llm; ai-guard, trial and prior-auth have one remote slot

**Proposed correction.** Say 'in each of the four configurations the pack supports', show unsupported arms as 'not applicable' rather than blank, and make A9 add the combined variant to the reference packs (a digest change with a rebuild).

### D7 (principles)

**The plan says.** A9 acceptance: a re-run with the same inputs and seeds is byte-identical (p.19)

**Why it is wrong.** Impossible for three of the four arms. Jev and LLM answers are not guaranteed repeatable (the default LLM does not even accept sampling parameters), and every report carries a random id, a wall-clock timestamp, measured latency and provider-reported cost. Even the offline arm differs between runs in id and latency.

- $ python det.py -> two runs on identical inputs differ in: id, latency_ms.max, latency_ms.mean, latency_ms.p50, latency_ms.p95
- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:199-200
- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:87-88 - 'Only for models that accept them (Claude Sonnet 5 rejects sampling parameters)'

### D8 (principles)

**The plan says.** A11.2: the shared payload includes confusion matrices and a dataset hash; A11.3: suppress any cell under 10 (the existing default) (p.20)

**Why it is wrong.** Three mismatches. The existing filter deliberately removes the dataset's name and hash and a test asserts it, so the prompt conflicts with a standing privacy rule and the shared header tells the session to stop on such a conflict. 'The existing default' covers only subgroup cells and calibration bins; confusion matrices, critical counts, a governance approver's name and the ids of missed critical cases pass through today, so the plan overstates what exists. And the two steps pull against each other: the error cells of a confusion matrix are nearly all under 10, so suppressing them literally removes the errors, while leaving row totals lets them be recovered.

- src/mendari/evals/share.py:38, 45 - the only two places MIN_GROUP is applied

**Proposed correction.** Decide the dataset-hash question explicitly (a keyed hash per site would allow de-duplication without a cross-site identifier). Rewrite A11.3 as a stated disclosure rule for every count in the payload (which cells are suppressed, how totals are protected), with the removal of missed_ids and of the governance override's names as named regression tests.

### D40 (today-claims)

**The plan says.** A9 ranking (p18): '1. Critical-label recall 2. False-automation rate', with neither metric defined

**Why it is wrong.** Both existing metrics mislead as ranking keys. The engine's false-automation rate counts only AUTO decisions whose primary label is wrong: the inbox run that automates 7 of 20 emergencies reports 0.0%. And per-label 'detection' can be low while every case is stopped: AI Guard's unsafe_advice=yes is 102/164 on its template set while all 164 drafts are blocked, so ranking first on that label would penalise a pack for a case its other slot caught.

**Proposed correction.** Define and rank on decision-level safety first: 'critical cases automated' (AUTO on any critical-positive case) and 'critical cases not escalated' (no review, block or stat priority), then per-label detection as a diagnostic, then the primary-label false-automation rate.

### D43 (today-claims)

**The plan says.** A9 and Part B: 'at least 100 positive cases per critical label' as the publication floor, with exact McNemar and Holm adjustment across arm pairs

**Why it is wrong.** Adequate as a floor, but with 100 positives a perfect 100/100 has an exact two-sided 95% lower bound of 0.964, so no grade can support a recall claim above about 96%. With four arms there are six pairwise tests; under Holm the smallest p-value must be below 0.0083, which exact McNemar reaches only with at least 8 discordant pairs all in one direction, so arms whose recall differs by fewer than about 8 points on 100 positives will tie and be ranked by later criteria.

- Clopper-Pearson lower bound for 100/100 = 0.025^(1/100) = 0.964 (hand computation)
- exact McNemar, all discordant pairs one way: p = 2 x 0.5^b; b=7 -> 0.0156, b=8 -> 0.0078; Holm threshold for the smallest of 6 = 0.05/6 = 0.0083 (hand computation)
- packs/clinical-trial-prescreener/evals/benchmark.json - 6 critical labels with 6 to 29 positives in 300 cases

**Proposed correction.** Publish the lower bound, not the point estimate, as the graded value; state the floor as a minimum for 'evidence', set a larger target (for example 300) for labels where a recall claim of 0.98 or more matters, and say in the method that most arm differences at n=100 will be reported as ties.

### D50 (partB-gates)

**The plan says.** 'target at least 100 positive cases per critical label' and '40-90 clinician-hours per pack' (p12), and A9 'a grade is published only when every critical label has at least 100 positive cases' (p18), with enriched sampling for emergencies

**Why it is wrong.** Statistically too weak for the claim it supports, the enrichment biases other metrics, and the hours estimate fits only a pack with one critical label. With 100 positives and zero misses the exact two-sided 95% lower bound on recall is 96.4%: the grade cannot exclude missing one emergency in 28. Showing recall of at least 99% needs about 368 positives with no miss (299 one-sided). A set enriched for emergencies no longer has natural prevalence, so false-automation rate, accuracy and calibration computed on it are not what a site would see unless results are reweighted by sampling fraction; the plan ranks on those metrics from the same sets. And the trial prescreener declares six critical labels, the rarest at 6 of 300 cases.

- $ python (re-run): 0.025**(1/100) -> 0.9638; ceil(ln 0.025 / ln 0.99) -> 368; ceil(ln 0.05 / ln 0.99) -> 299
- $ python: 23/600 -> 0.0383, 100/0.0383 -> 2609 (the plan's 2,600 is right for the inbox pack)
- $ python over packs/*/evals/benchmark.json -> critical positives 23 (inbox), 25 (prior-auth), 13/6/17/13/29/17 (trial)

**Proposed correction.** Define the publication rule by the interval: publish when the Clopper-Pearson lower bound on each critical label's recall clears a stated floor, and show the bound. Record each case's sampling stratum and report prevalence-dependent metrics reweighted to the natural mix (or on a separate natural-prevalence stratum). Budget labelling hours per critical label.

### D59 (A1)

### D74 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 1: 'a pack may name only a provider type and variant.'

**Why it is wrong.** Not implementable as written, and weaker on privacy if taken literally. Local providers need pack configuration (rules file, model file, text fields), and remote variants carry `state_fields`, the data-minimisation control. The real gap is narrower: the pack still picks the LLM model (and so the vendor behind the gateway) and the spend, and sets its own Jev price.

- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:78-91,114 - pack-settable fields; the pack's model wins

### D75 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 1: 'Validation rejects any pack field that names an environment variable, a secret, a header or a URL.'

**Why it is wrong.** Taken literally it refuses every shipped pack: each input schema names two URLs (`$schema`, `$id`), four packs name a FHIR code-system URL in their mapping, and the spec gives packs `publisher.url`, `card.evidence[].url` and prefetch templates. The harm is a field that changes where a request goes or which credential is attached, not a URL as such.

- $ git grep -c -E 'https?://' -- 'packs/*/schemas/*.json' 'packs/*/fhir/*.yaml' -> 2 in each of the five input schemas, 1 in each of four mapping.yaml files
- packs/patient-inbox-router/fhir/mapping.yaml:31 - performer_system: https://mendari.co/fhir/CodeSystem/inbox-destination
- src/mendari/core/spec.py:92-107,461 - publisher.url, evidence.url and prefetch are part of the manifest model

**Proposed correction.** 'Validation rejects any provider or hook field that can change where a request is sent or which credential or header is attached; every other URL a pack may carry is listed by field, must be https (or a relative FHIR read or search for prefetch) and is never fetched.'

### D76 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 1: 'All outbound calls go through the existing allow-list.'

**Why it is wrong.** The existing allow-list is the FHIR-origin guard for servers that requests name (SSRF). Model-provider, Vercel Connect, webhook and registry destinations are deployment constants and were never on it. Literal compliance would mean adding the AI Gateway to MENDARI_FHIR_ALLOWED_SERVERS, which would also make it a legal CDS Hooks fhirServer and SMART EHR base: a wider attack surface, not a narrower one.

- src/mendari/standards/fhir_client.py:1-14,38-58 - the list is for FHIR servers 'someone else named'
- src/mendari/providers/http.py:41-59 - provider calls: https check only
- src/mendari/server/smart_check.py:65-69 and src/mendari/standards/smart.py:99-100 - the same list authorizes SMART EHR bases

**Proposed correction.** 'Pack-driven calls go only to destinations fixed in server configuration. Add a separate provider egress allow-list (defaulting to the configured endpoints' origins) enforced in one outbound helper; the FHIR allow-list stays for FHIR.'

### D77 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 2: 'evaluate every pack pattern with a linear-time engine (google-re2).'

**Why it is wrong.** Underspecified to the point of changing clinical behaviour. RE2 is not a drop-in for the pack dialect: 4 shipped patterns use lookaround and would not compile, 53 use \b and 36 use \w, \s or \d, whose Unicode meaning differs in RE2, 2 hold non-ASCII (Spanish) literals, and jsonschema runs `pattern` and `patternProperties` on `re` regardless. Rewriting red-flag patterns changes pack digests, benchmarks and possibly emergency detection, which the shared header forbids weakening. The repository's own notes (leads) say a second regex engine with a time budget was already tried and dropped; they do not say google-re2 was the one tried.

- $ python skeptic/shipped.py -> 104 patterns: 4 with lookaround (ai-guard, clinical-trial-prescreener x2, referral-router), 53 with \b, 36 with \w, \s or \d, 2 with non-ASCII literals
- tasks/todo.md:269-272 - 'the regex-engine approach was tried and dropped ... could not match `re`'s semantics exactly, its clock was the process's, and its tables slowed every start' (lead)
- src/mendari/core/decision.py:250 - schema patterns run inside jsonschema

**Proposed correction.** State the outcome and let the build choose the mechanism: 'No pack-authored evaluation can take more than N ms of CPU on a 10,000-character input.' Accept either RE2 with a pinned dialect in a new spec version, a conformance run over all reference datasets (identical decisions, or version bumps with regenerated benchmarks and cards) and a custom jsonschema pattern keyword; or process isolation with a CPU limit. Require the owner to pick before the session starts.

### D78 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 2 as a whole: patterns are the only way a pack ties up the server.

**Why it is wrong.** They are not, so RE2 alone would leave the goal ('an untrusted pack cannot ... tie up the server') unmet. Measured: a 3 KB input schema with no pattern (two internal `$ref`s under `allOf` per level) is accepted and stalls a decision on a 13-character message; a wording template's format width allocates 260 MiB per card; Mendari's own regex over a pack's CQL text is quadratic and runs inside the health request; one pattern within the caps takes 1.45 s to compile.

- $ python skeptic/schema_fanout.py -> depth 14: decide 0.43 s CPU; depth 28 (2,952 bytes): load accepted in 0.03 s, decide KILLED at 20 s
- $ python skeptic/template_child.py 200000000 -> validate rc 0, peak RSS 260 MiB (72 at width 100)
- $ python skeptic/health_probe.py cql 60000 -> first /api/health 3.51 s
- $ python skeptic/compile_cost.py -> 1,990-character pattern: compile 1.45 s

**Proposed correction.** Word step 2 as a budget on all pack-authored work (schema validation, patterns, templates, provider construction, loading), with size and depth caps on pack files, and make the tests include a pattern-free case.

### D79 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 2: 'Add a per-decision CPU budget.'

**Why it is wrong.** It does not say how, and the obvious ways do not work in this server: a backtracking `re` match holds the GIL, so a watchdog thread never runs (observed), and signal-based timeouts reach only the main thread while FastAPI runs sync routes in worker threads. It also names CPU only, while remote providers burn wall-clock (an LLM variant may wait 120 s plus a retry) and templates can burn memory.

- $ python skeptic/health_probe.py during -> after the pathological decide started in a thread, the main thread never ran again before the 20 s kill
- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:82,196 - timeout_ms up to 120000; retries=1
- $ python skeptic/template_child.py 200000000 -> validate ok; peak RSS 260 MiB against 72

**Proposed correction.** 'Run pack-authored evaluation for packs not owned by the deployment in a worker process with CPU-time and memory limits and a parent-side kill; add a wall-clock deadline across providers. A blown budget is a provider failure, so the policy falls back to a person.'

### D80 (A3)

**The plan says.** Step 2: 'The health check must never evaluate pack patterns.'

**Why it is wrong.** Too narrow to deliver its purpose: the sentence is already true and health is still stallable. The measured stalls come from building providers inside the request (Mendari's own quadratic regex over a pack's CQL text, repeated on every call when the build fails) and from the GIL being held elsewhere, not from evaluating a pack pattern.

- src/mendari/server/app.py:585-587 - health calls decision_for for every served pack
- $ python skeptic/health_probe.py cql -> 396 KiB padded library: first /api/health killed at 20 s; 64 KiB: 3.51 s
- $ python skeptic/health_repeat.py 40000 -> 1.5 s on each of four health calls

**Proposed correction.** 'The health check does no pack-dependent work: it reports pack state computed at startup or in the background, and answers within a fixed bound whatever packs are installed.'

### D81 (A3)

**The plan says.** Tests: 'finish within 50 ms' on six named patterns.

**Why it is wrong.** A wall-clock threshold on shared CI runners is flaky, and six examples prove nothing about the next pattern. The owner's own shipped patterns already miss the bar under `re`: one crafted 10,000-character message costs the unmodified inbox pack 563 ms, so the test as written fails on reference packs unless scoped.

- $ python skeptic/shipped_decide.py -> 563.0 ms CPU at 10,000 characters, 150.1 at 5,000, 37.9 at 2,500 (quadratic)
- $ python skeptic/shipped.py -> gi-bleeding 599.5 ms, coughing-blood 367.0 ms, pregnancy-bleeding 336.2 ms on crude 10,000-character texts

**Proposed correction.** Assert CPU time with headroom or linear scaling (10,000 against 100,000 characters), over a generated family of nested-quantifier patterns plus every shipped pattern, for rules patterns, schema `pattern` and `patternProperties` keys, and one pattern-free schema.

### D86 (A4)

**The plan says.** p.10 goal: 'no configuration can automate a missed emergency', with acceptance 'the rules-only AUTO test passes'.

**Why it is wrong.** The fix and its acceptance test prove only that configurations without a model in the screen never automate. The evidence for the allowed configurations is 20 held-out emergencies (48 with the tuning set): with 0 misses in 20 the one-sided 95% upper bound on the miss rate is still about 14% (about 6% for 0 in 48), and those rows are leads measured on 2026-09-28, not re-run here. The only gate in the repository compares the template benchmark set, on which every configuration scores 23/23. The goal as written is unprovable and overstates what ships.

### D89 (A4)

**The plan says.** p.10 item 1: 'regenerate its Decision Card and benchmark' as a routine build step.

**Why it is wrong.** The card's provider comparison is read from evals/leaderboard.json: 28 rows measured on 0.3.0, most from live Jev and LLM calls. A build session under the shared header (synthetic only, no hosted calls) cannot re-run them, rows carry pack_version but no digest, are replaced only per (configuration, dataset), and the card prints them without their version. A regenerated 0.4.0 card would therefore still show '4/20 (7 automated)' and automation rates for configurations whose behaviour the version bump changes (rules-only, and model-only screens, which the allowed list also stops automating). This is already happening: four other reference packs ship cards whose rows were measured on an older pack version. ### D96 (A5)

**The plan says.** A5 step 3: add key rotation for the input-hash key by re-keying in batches, with verify still passing (p.10).

**Why it is wrong.** Infeasible as worded. The keyed hash is a field of the decision record, and the record's SHA-256 is chained at decision.created, so rewriting an old hash breaks `audit verify`. In hash mode, and after retention in encrypt mode, the input needed to recompute the hash no longer exists.

- src/mendari/core/decision.py:100 - input_hash is in the record
- src/mendari/core/audit.py:401 and 1835-1838 - record_sha256 is chained and re-checked by verify
- $ python s3_guard_keys.py, part (d) -> after rewriting one stored input_hash: verify ok False, broken_at 2
- docs/deploying-with-phi.md:354-355 - LEAD: records keep the old key's id and are never re-hashed

**Proposed correction.** Split step 3. PHI key: batched re-encryption with a key ring and a key id in the ciphertext. Input-hash key: rotation means a new key id for new records plus a chained rotation event; old hashes are never rewritten. If replaceable old hashes are required, first decide to move input_hash out of the chained record for new records.

### D97 (A5)

**The plan says.** A5's five steps make the hosted site store 'nothing it can't protect or erase' (p.10), given that today inputs are 'stored in plaintext, can't be erased' (p.3).

**Why it is wrong.** The steps only change how new decisions are stored. Plaintext already inside chained records stays readable by any principal with `read` after the switch to encrypt or hash, is never purged, and cannot be removed without breaking verify. The acceptance criterion fails on that data.

- $ python s2_routes.py legacy -> a viewer key in encrypt mode reads legacy plaintext from /api/audit, /api/audit/{id}, /api/review and /api/feedback with +0 input.read
- $ python s3_guard_keys.py, part (e) -> the purge deletes 0; setting record.input to null by hand breaks verify
- src/mendari/core/audit.py:1000-1003 and 1022-1026

**Proposed correction.** Add a step 0: retire or migrate the existing hosted database (owner decision), and gate record-held inputs on the read side in hash and encrypt modes. State the acceptance criterion for both new and pre-existing rows.

### D100 (A5)

**The plan says.** A5 step 2: schedule the retention purge with Vercel cron (one line).

**Why it is wrong.** Vercel cron is an HTTP GET to a path on the production deployment. The repository has no such route; a GET under /api/ without its own rule is open to every principal that may read; the guard refuses any Bearer credential that is not an API key or access token; the purge runs unbounded in one transaction under the chain lock; and cron does not run on preview deployments. The prompt names none of this.

- src/mendari/core/audit.py:1016-1029
- vercel.json:8-13 - maxDuration 300

### D108 (A5)

**The plan says.** Purge and erase make data gone (A5 goal and acceptance).

**Why it is wrong.** On the hosted stack a deleted row persists in the database's point-in-time history, in backups, in any preview branch made before the purge, and in earlier exports. The plan sets no bound on any of these, and a 30-day promise in the privacy notice would be false if the history window or a long-lived preview branch outlasts it.

**The plan says.** p2 table: hosted platform is 'Owner only, one shared organization'; blockers 'No accounts or organizations ... no self-service keys'

### D111 (A6)

**The plan says.** A6 item 5: 'Per-user daily caps alongside the existing per-organization quotas, with a 429 and Retry-After when exceeded'

**Why it is wrong.** The existing organization quota does not answer 429 on a decision: over quota the decision is made, recorded and returned 200 as ABSTAIN or HUMAN_REVIEW (the 'policy only lowers automation' design, with a test). The prompt would create two opposite behaviours for the same kind of limit without saying so. A 429 on clinical entry points (CDS Hooks, the EHR launch) shows the clinician nothing, whereas the current fallback still routes the case to a person. It does not say who a 'user' is (people, keys, clients, EHR launches) or which actions are capped, it ignores that evaluations bypass organization quotas, and it overlooks that a per-principal 429 with Retry-After already exists and already accepts a 24-hour window, so the real work is a second, daily rate beside the per-minute one.

- src/mendari/server/limits.py:94-102 - one Rate per class

**Proposed correction.** Specify: a daily cap per principal id (user:, key:, client:, ehr:), kept beside the per-minute rates, checked before any work, 429 with Retry-After to local midnight and nothing recorded, on evaluation, guard, export and sandbox decide routes; for clinical entry points state explicitly whether the cap refuses or falls back to human review, and make organization quotas follow the same documented rule. Add per-organization accounting of evaluation provider calls and a cap on active keys per organization.

**Why it is wrong.** In the code 'default' is the catch-all, not a private organization: a sign-in without an organization claim, rows with no organization, open mode and every write without context all resolve to it, and the docs tell every single-organization site to register its EHR to 'default'. **Why it is wrong.** Taken literally it is unsafe and incomplete. The mapping is the owner's own admin access, and the hosted platform has no shell to repair a lockout. **The plan says.** A6 item 1 and the goal: organizations in the data model; 'each partner team works in its own organization without the owner's help'

It does not say who creates an organization and its first admin in stages 2 to 4 (self sign-up of an organization is stage 5, p14, so until then somebody must: presumably the owner, which is the owner's help once per partner), what an organization id may be, or that 'default' is reserved. The code today takes the id as free text from a claim and checks a pattern only for EHR registrations.

**Why it is wrong.** These are one designed behaviour, not two bugs: a scoped credential reaches only routes that name a scope. The rule is written in server/scopes.py, stated in the deployment guide and pinned by an exact test oracle (ADR-0004 defines the scope language it rests on). Calling it a bug to fix, without saying the oracle, the guide and the decision record change, invites a build session to hit the shared header's 'conflicts with the code' stop. It also misses the wider case: SMART Backend Services tokens are always scoped, so no token can read CDS discovery or list packs.

- src/mendari/server/auth.py:618

### D119 (A6)

**The plan says.** A6 acceptance 1: 'generated tests call every route as two organizations and assert no cross-organization data in any response'

### D122 (A7)

**The plan says.** A7.3: 'label set equal to the pack's declared answers, minimum 50 cases per label to run an evaluation'.

**Why it is wrong.** Every reference pack's own benchmark test set fails both rules, so the reference packs could not be evaluated in the store and the acceptance flow has no shipped dataset to use. Critical labels are rare by nature (23 urgent cases of 600 in the inbox set), and several declared labels such as `unknown` have zero cases. The rule also disagrees with A9, which uses 100 positives per critical label as a bar for publishing a grade, not for running an evaluation.

### D123 (A7)

**The plan says.** A7.3: 'duplicate detection' (unspecified) and a hash check only against hidden sets.

**Why it is wrong.** The plan does not say what a duplicate is or what happens when one is found, and it has no check for test cases that also appear in the pack's own training or calibration data. The shipped data already shows both problems, so point metrics are inflated and any interval computed on the row count would be too narrow.

- $ packs/ai-guard/data/test.jsonl (re-run): 600 rows, 81 unique inputs (largest group 35); 72 of the 81 also appear in calibration.jsonl
- $ packs/patient-inbox-router/data (re-run): test shares 20 inputs with train and 4 with calibration; 9 duplicate rows inside test

**Proposed correction.** Define a duplicate as an equal canonical-JSON input (plus a normalized-text variant). ### D124 (A7)

**The plan says.** A7.3: PHI detection applies to 'test-data upload', with a deterministic detector for names, dates of birth, MRNs, phone numbers and addresses and an unspecified threshold.

**Why it is wrong.** A signed pack archive carries its own data/*.jsonl, tests/cases.yaml and examples, so PHI can arrive through A7.2's upload without touching the test-data path. A deterministic detector cannot find names reliably, and a naive date rule would reject the reference data: 54% of shipped synthetic cases contain a date-like string and about 1% a title-plus-name string, while none contains a phone, MRN, SSN, email or street-address pattern. Without a stated threshold and a corpus to tune against, the check will either block legitimate synthetic data or be presented as a guarantee it cannot give.

- src/mendari/hub/archive.py:114-122, 130-141 - the archive includes every non-hidden file of the pack, data and tests included
- $ pattern counts over packs/*/data/*.jsonl and datasets/*.jsonl (27 files, 8,840 cases; verifier's own regexes, same totals as the first audit): date-like 4,758; title+name 105; phone-like 0; MRN 0; street-address-like 0; birth-date key or wording 0; SSN-like 0; email 0

**Proposed correction.** Scan archive contents as well as test-data files. Specify the detector: structural identifiers (phone, MRN, SSN, email, street address, birth-date fields and dates next to birth words) reject on one hit; names are reported as warnings. Make zero rejections on all shipped synthetic data a CI test, and describe the check as a screen that backs the synthetic-only terms, not as proof of no PHI.

### D125 (A7)

**The plan says.** A7.4: each metric 'with confidence intervals (methods in A9), plus a paired comparison of the two versions'.

**Why it is wrong.** Four gaps. (1) A9 gives exact Clopper-Pearson for proportions and a bootstrap for ECE and Brier, but names no method for macro-F1, which is not a proportion and needs a bootstrap. (2) The false-automation rate's denominator is the number of AUTO decisions, which differs between versions (567 against 574 in the measured draft), so McNemar cannot be run on the rate; it must be run on a per-case indicator over all cases. (3) A9 asks for ECE on equal-mass bins while the code and the drift monitor use equal-width tenths; changing the bins would move every published ECE and break the monitor's PSI, which reads the benchmark's bins as tenths. (4) A significance test is the wrong rule for safety regressions: 3 new false automations against 0 gives exact McNemar p = 0.25, which A9's rule calls a tie, and the current tolerance rule also passes it.

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:226-227 - false_automation_rate = wrong AUTO / AUTO; false_automation_share = wrong AUTO / all cases
- src/mendari/evals/metrics.py:52 - 'equal-width confidence bins'; src/mendari/evals/monitoring.py:146-160 - _psi places each benchmark bin by round(low * 10)
- $ mendari eval draft --dataset test --baseline out/current.json -> 3 of 574 false automations, 'No degradation beyond tolerance (3.0 pts)' (re-run)
- verifier's calculation: exact McNemar, 0 against 3 discordant -> p = 0.25; plan p.18 - 'A difference that isn't significant after adjustment is a tie'; plan p.18 statistics list has no line for macro-F1
- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:255-265 - reports keep at most 50 misclassified ids and no per-case result vector

**Proposed correction.** State per metric: Clopper-Pearson for accuracy, per-label recall, false-automation share and automation rate; seeded bootstrap for macro-F1, ECE and Brier; exact McNemar on per-case indicators over the same cases. Keep the equal-width ECE and add the equal-mass one beside it. For safety metrics use a one-sided non-regression rule and list every newly false-automated or newly automated critical case by id; never treat 'not significant' as acceptable there. Require matching dataset sha256 and store per-case result rows (ids only).

### D128 (A7)

**The plan says.** A7.6: 'Export reviewers' corrections from the review queue into an improvement dataset for the pack.'

**Why it is wrong.** Added by the verifier. The plan does not say which deployment's review queue feeds the dataset or where the dataset may go, and the two readings conflict with its own principles. On the hosted platform the sandbox is synthetic-only (p.2), so the queue holds synthetic cases and the corrections teach little. The corrections worth having are made at sites on real messages, and the current export writes each case's full input and the rater's free-text note; such a file cannot be uploaded to the hosted store, because A7.3 must reject PHI-like data and the plan says sites share metrics only.

- src/mendari/server/app.py:1071-1097 - the export route returns those records as a JSONL download

**Proposed correction.** Say that the improvement export is produced and kept where the review queue lives. On the hosted sandbox it may feed a draft directly. At a site it stays on the site's servers and feeds the local loop (`mendari eval`, `mendari test`); only metrics leave, through A11. Run every export through the A7.3 PHI screen before it can be attached to a hosted draft, and leave free-text notes out by default.

### D129 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 2: report Cohen's kappa per question with a bootstrap 95% interval (2,000 resamples, fixed seed), plus raw percent agreement (p17).

**Why it is wrong.** Underspecified to the point of giving misleading numbers. (1) Cohen's kappa is defined for one fixed pair of raters; with a pool of clinicians the pair changes from case to case. (2) Kappa collapses on rare labels, and p12 requires enriched sampling, so kappa will not be comparable between sets or with deployment prevalence. (3) A bootstrap resample in which both raters use a single category has kappa undefined; with few positives this will happen. (4) It does not say agreement is computed on the two blind first-pass labels rather than after adjudication. (5) Several critical labels sit on derived questions, which are computed from other answers.

- $ python primary.py -> inbox test urgency: routine 577, urgent 23 (3.8%); trial hold-out positives per critical label 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 0
- packs/ai-guard/pack.yaml:168 and packs/referral-router/pack.yaml:151 - verdict and next_step are derived; both carry critical labels (ai-guard pack.yaml:262, referral pack.yaml:263)
- $ python counts.py -> questions labelled per record: ai-guard 7, trial 12, prior-auth 9, referral 9, inbox 2

**Proposed correction.** Per question: percent agreement; Cohen's kappa per rater pair and a pooled chance-corrected coefficient valid for varying pairs (Krippendorff's alpha, nominal); positive and negative specific agreement with exact intervals for each critical label. Bootstrap over cases, seeded, with the rule for undefined resamples written down and the count of such resamples reported. First-pass labels only. Clinicians label the member questions; derived answers are computed with the pack's table, and where clinicians also label the derived answer, report its consistency.

### D130 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 3: lifecycle draft, frozen, active, retired; 'only frozen sets can grade'; 'active sets are never returned'; acceptance 'freezing changes nothing in the content hash afterwards' (p17).

**Why it is wrong.** Ambiguous and, read literally, inconsistent. If only frozen sets can grade, an active set cannot, yet active is the state the grading service is said to read. Secrecy is stated only for active sets, so a draft or frozen set would be readable until it is activated. The acceptance sentence does not say what must stay true (freezing is what computes the hash).

- plan p17, A8 item 3 and the acceptance paragraph (launch-plan.txt lines 561-565 and 570-572)
- src/mendari/server/auth.py:174 - today any role with `read` reaches every unlisted GET /api/ route, so an unprotected draft set would be visible to every signed-in user

**Proposed correction.** States: draft (mutable, secret) -> frozen (immutable, secret, hash signed) -> active (frozen and in use for grading) -> retired (may be published). Grading is allowed in frozen and active. Secrecy applies to draft, frozen and active. Acceptance: after freeze every write is refused and the recomputed content hash equals the signed one at activation, at every grading read and at retirement.

### D131 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 4, p12 and A9: a critical label needs at least 100 positive cases.

**Why it is wrong.** It does not say distinct or independent cases. A template-generated set reaches 100 by repetition, and exact binomial intervals assume independent trials. The repository's own largest positive counts are mostly repeats.

- $ python counts.py -> ai-guard test: verdict=block 164 rows / 30 distinct inputs; dose_exceeds_limit=yes 62 rows / 4 distinct; n=600 with 81 distinct inputs
- $ python facts2.py -> ai-guard test rows identical to a calibration input: 573 of 600
- $ python ref.py -> referral test urgent rows 113, distinct reason texts 70, rows whose reason text also occurs in an urgent train case 72

**Proposed correction.** Require 100 distinct positives after exact and near-duplicate removal, at most k cases per template or author, and report the effective sample size beside the raw count. A set that reaches 100 only through repeats shows 'insufficient evidence'.

### D132 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 4 lists 'synthetic generator' as a source of hidden-set cases (p17), and p1 open-sources the engine and reference packs at stage 3.

**Why it is wrong.** A case drawn from the repository's generators is not hidden once the code is public. The generators and their template banks ship in the package, the splits are reproducible byte for byte from a seed, and a new seed only re-samples the same templates. A developer can fit to the template bank, which is why template sets score 0.97-1.0. The plan never says hidden cases must come from somewhere else.

- src/mendari/sandbox/synthetic_inbox.py:599-609 and 674-676 - cases are sampled from the module's TEMPLATES by a seeded random.Random; splits are slices of one run
- $ python facts2.py -> regenerated test == committed: True 600
- pyproject.toml:65 - /src (with mendari/sandbox) is in the sdist
- $ python facts2.py and ref.py -> test rows whose text also occurs in the fitting data: ai-guard 573 of 600 (identical input), referral 516 of 600 (reason text), trial 226 of 300, prior-auth 265 of 600, inbox 131 of 600

**Proposed correction.** State that no hidden case may come from a public generator or template bank. If generated cases are wanted, they need a private template bank kept with the hidden-set store, and the coverage report must list template ids and cap cases per template.

### D133 (A8)

**The plan says.** p12: 'emergencies need enriched sampling' to reach 100 positives; A9 then ranks on false-automation rate, accuracy and calibration from the same sets.

**Why it is wrong.** Statistically unsound as written. Enrichment changes prevalence, so every prevalence-dependent metric (accuracy, false-automation rate, automation rate, ECE, Brier) measured on the enriched set is biased relative to real case mix; only per-label recall is unaffected. The plan also does not say how positives are found: if a model or the pack's own rules pre-screen candidates, the set is biased toward cases those systems already catch.

- plan p12 (launch-plan.txt lines 362-364); metric list on p17-18
- $ python primary.py -> natural urgent rate in the synthetic inbox data: 23/600 (test), 69/1500 (train), 18/400 (local site)

**Proposed correction.** A8 item 4 records each case's stratum and sampling weight; A9 reports recall on the enriched stratum and prevalence-dependent metrics either on a natural-mix stratum or weighted back to a stated prevalence. Enrichment must come from authors or chart review blind to any graded system, never from a model's flags.

### D134 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 3 third bullet and acceptance 1: 'active sets are never returned by any API, export or log' is enough to keep a set hidden (p17); A7 item 3 rejects any uploaded case matching a hidden set (p16); A9 runs +Jev and +LLM arms on the hidden sets and gives developers a log of every run (p17-18).

**Why it is wrong.** Three leaks remain that the acceptance test would not catch. (1) Grading results: today's report format names misclassified cases with their true label and lists missed critical case ids. (2) The A7 rejection is a membership oracle: a developer learns that a guessed case is in the hidden set; a plain hash of short structured inputs can also be reversed by guessing, as the code's own comment says. (3) Every +Jev or +LLM run sends each hidden case's input to an outside provider. Repeated submissions also let a developer fit to the hidden set; A9 limits re-runs per version but not the number of versions.

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:180-184 and 255-265 - missed_ids and misclassified {id, truth, predicted}
- $ python facts2.py -> shareable critical keys include 'missed_ids'; missed_ids kept: 16
- src/mendari/core/phi.py:20-25 - 'A plain SHA-256 of a short or structured input can be found by guessing'
- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:49 (GATEWAY_URL, an outside AI gateway) and src/mendari/providers/jev.py:147-156 (the request body with the case inputs is sent to the configured Jev endpoint)

**Proposed correction.** Add to A8: an aggregates-only result shape for hidden sets; a keyed-HMAC case index for the A7 check, with matches quarantined silently rather than rejected with a reason; an exposure ledger per set and provider with a retirement threshold, and zero-retention terms before any hidden case is sent to a provider; a submission budget per developer per set; canary strings in hidden cases.

### D135 (A8)

**The plan says.** p1 calls the hidden sets 'rotating'; A8 item 3 only names a retired state.

**Why it is wrong.** Nothing in A8 or A9 says when a set is rotated or how grades stay comparable across set versions. Without a rotation trigger a set is used until it leaks; without linking cases shared by the old and new versions, a pack's grade changes with the set and nobody can tell whether the pack or the set moved.

- plan p1 (launch-plan.txt line 20) against p17 (lines 561-565): no rotation rule
- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:211-216 - a report identifies its dataset only by name and file hash; there is no set version or link between versions

**Proposed correction.** Add a rotation rule to A8 (a maximum number of grading runs or provider exposures, or a maximum age, whichever comes first) and a linking design: each new set version keeps a fixed share of anchor cases from the previous one, and grades name the set version.

### D136 (A8)

**The plan says.** A8 item 1 third bullet (every label is chained in the audit trail) together with item 3 third bullet (active sets are never returned by any API, export or log).

**Why it is wrong.** The two pull against each other and the plan does not say how to reconcile them. Today's chained label events (review.resolved, feedback.recorded) carry the label in the clear, and chained events are served to `read` and `admin` roles through the audit routes and the FHIR export, none of which is the grading service. A label event built the same way would put a hidden set's answers where acceptance 1 says they must never appear; a build that keeps labels out of the chain would fail item 1.
