### D143 (A9)

**The plan says.** Within each arm, search the declared provider variants and report the best configuration (p17), ranked on the same hidden set.

**Why it is wrong.** Choosing the best of k variants on the set that also ranks it is selection on the test set: the reported figure is the maximum of k noisy estimates, biased upward, and its interval under-covers. As an upper bound (k variants with independent errors, 100 positives, true recall 0.95) the expected best-of-6 recall is 0.976 and best-of-9 is 0.979; the chance the best shows 100/100 rises from 0.6% (k=1) to 3.5% (k=6) and 5.2% (k=9), and a 100/100 winner's Clopper-Pearson lower bound (0.964) excludes the truth. Variants run on the same cases are positively correlated, so the real optimism is smaller, but it is never zero. The shipped leaderboards already hold 6 LLM-arm rows per dataset. 'Best' is also undefined: best by the lexicographic rule needs the tie rule, which is itself ill-defined.

- $ scratch stats.py -> 'n=100 p=.95 k=6: E[max]=0.9757 P(max=100/100)=0.0350'; 'k=9: 0.9794, 0.0520'; 'k=1: 0.9500, 0.0059'; 'CP 100/100: [0.9638, 1.0000]'
- $ scratch scan.py -> '+llm': 6 rows on every dataset of every pack

**Proposed correction.** Sample splitting: split each frozen set by a hash of the case id, stratified by critical label, into a selection part and a ranking part; pick the variant on the first and report it on the second. Or have the submitter declare one configuration per arm before grading (selection then happens on the author's own public data). If one set must serve both, report every variant and give the selected one a Bonferroni-adjusted Clopper-Pearson interval at level 1 - 0.05/k, which is valid under any dependence between variants.

### D144 (A9)

**The plan says.** A difference that isn't significant after adjustment is a tie and passes to the next criterion (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** 'Not significantly different' is not transitive, so the rule does not define an order and can produce cycles. Example with 100 positives and nested misses: A 100/100, B 96/100, C 92/100. Exact McNemar: A vs B p=0.125 (tie), B vs C p=0.125 (tie), A vs C p=0.0078 (A better; below the Holm threshold 0.0167 for the smallest of 3). If B beats A and C beats B on false automation, the rule gives C > B > A > C. The rule also treats absence of evidence as equivalence: with few positives almost everything ties on safety, so the rank is decided by accuracy on the larger sample and the safety criterion stops mattering.

- $ scratch stats.py -> 'McNemar b,c: (4,0) 0.125 ... (8,0) 0.0078125 | 0.05/3 = 0.0167'

**Proposed correction.** Banded lexicographic order with rank intervals. (1) Absolute safety gates first: each critical label's Clopper-Pearson lower bound at or above a pre-registered threshold, and zero automated critical cases; arms that fail are listed unranked. (2) Map each criterion to bands fixed before any data is seen, using its conservative bound (lower for recall, upper for false automation). 'Same band' is an equivalence relation, so the lexicographic sort on band tuples is a well-defined total preorder; arms with equal tuples share a rank. The cost is a discontinuity at band edges, which should be stated. (3) Show uncertainty as a 95% confidence set for each arm's rank (Mogstad, Romano, Shaikh and Wilhelm 2024; Hall and Miller 2009), built from the paired per-case results; for recall near 100% use exact or Beta-posterior draws, because resampling a 100/100 result never varies. (4) Keep Holm-adjusted pairwise tests as annotations, never as the sort key.

### D145 (A9)

**The plan says.** A grade is published when every critical label has at least 100 positive cases (p18), and arms are ranked by significant differences in critical-label recall.

**Why it is wrong.** 100 positives support only coarse claims. Exact 95% intervals: 100/100 gives [0.964, 1.000]; 99/100 [0.946, 1.000]; 95/100 [0.887, 0.984]. A perfect score cannot show recall above 96.4%, and one miss drops the bound below 95%. Exact McNemar needs at least 6 one-sided discordant positives for p<0.05 and at least 8 once Holm divides alpha across 6 arm pairs, whatever the correlation between arms, so recall differences under 6-8 points can never be declared. With independent errors, power for 0.99 vs 0.95 is 20% unadjusted and 5% adjusted; 0.99 vs 0.90 is 77% and 50%; 0.95 vs 0.85 is 58% and 32%. The rule also covers recall only: a grade could publish with a handful of automated decisions behind the false-automation rate.

- $ scratch stats.py -> 'CP 100/100: [0.9638, 1.0000]', 'CP 99/100: [0.9455, 0.9997]', 'CP 95/100: [0.8872, 0.9836]'
- $ scratch stats.py -> 'McNemar (6,0) 0.03125; (7,0) 0.015625; (8,0) 0.0078125 | 0.05/6 = 0.00833'
- $ scratch stats.py -> 'power n=100 0.99 vs 0.95: alpha .05 -> 0.20; alpha .05/6 -> 0.05'; '0.99 vs 0.9: 0.77; 0.50'; '0.95 vs 0.85: 0.58; 0.32'; 'n=400 0.99 vs 0.95: 0.91; 0.74'
- $ scratch stats.py -> 'zero-miss n for lower >= .95/.97/.99: [72, 122, 368]'

**Proposed correction.** State the claim the grade makes and size for it: publish the Clopper-Pearson lower bound as the headline ('at least X% with 95% confidence'), and set the minimum from the target bound (122 zero-miss positives for 0.97, 368 for 0.99). Use enriched (case-control) sampling of critical positives to reach the count, and weight prevalence-dependent metrics back by inverse sampling probability. Add a minimum for automated decisions too (for example at least 300 AUTO cases before a false-automation bound is published). Publish a power table with the method.

### D146 (A9)

**The plan says.** Holm-adjusted across the pairs of arms, alpha 0.05 (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** The family is larger than the 6 arm pairs. Each scoreboard tests every pair on every ranking criterion and on every critical label (trial has 6 critical labels, ai-guard 4), on two sets (held-out and shifted), for every pack. Adjusting within one criterion only leaves the scoreboard-wide error rate far above 5%. The intervals are unadjusted, so a reader scanning many 95% intervals will see some exclude the truth by chance. Macro-F1, cost and latency are reported or ranked with no interval or test specified at all.

- packs/clinical-trial-prescreener/pack.yaml:314-320 - six critical labels
- packs/ai-guard/pack.yaml:261-265 - four critical labels
- launch-plan p18 - statistics listed only for proportions, ECE and Brier

**Proposed correction.** Define the family in the method: per pack and set, all arm pairs x all ranking criteria x all critical labels, Holm over the whole family (or a fixed-sequence gatekeeping procedure that follows the ranking order). Across packs, control the false discovery rate with Benjamini-Yekutieli. Give the critical labels of one arm simultaneous intervals (Clopper-Pearson at 1 - 0.05/L). Specify a stratified bootstrap interval for macro-F1, compute cost from tokens and a dated price table, and leave latency unranked.

### D147 (A9)

**The plan says.** Developer flow: submit a pack version, receive the scoreboard, request one re-run per version (p18), against fixed hidden sets.

**Why it is wrong.** One re-run per version does not bound the number of versions. Each scoreboard is feedback about the hidden set; a developer who submits many versions and keeps the best is fitting the set (adaptive overfitting). As an upper bound (independent versions, each truly at 0.95 recall on 100 positives) the best of 20 is expected to show 0.986 and the best of 50 shows 0.991; accuracy on 600 cases at a true 0.90 gains about 2.2 points over 20 versions. Versions of one pack are correlated, so the real gain is smaller, but nothing in the plan caps it. Returning per-case detail makes it worse: today's report format returns the ids of missed critical cases and up to 50 misclassified cases with their true labels.

- $ scratch stats.py -> 'n=100 p=.95 k=20: E[max]=0.9856'; 'k=50: E[max]=0.9910'; 'n=600 p=0.9 k=20: E[max]=0.9222'
- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:180-184,255-265 - missed_ids and misclassified with truth and prediction in every report

**Proposed correction.** Budget graded submissions per organization and pack lineage per set rotation (for example 5 per quarter), not per version. Return banded results only, with thresholding in the style of Thresholdout or the Ladder mechanism (Dwork et al. 2015; Blum and Hardt 2015), and never per-case fields. Keep a sealed confirmation split that a pack lineage is scored on once before a grade is published, and rotate a fixed share of each set every quarter (the plan calls the sets 'rotating' on p1, but A9 never uses rotation).

### D148 (A9)

**The plan says.** A re-run with the same inputs and seeds is byte-identical (p19); record every model version per run (p17).

**Why it is wrong.** Jev and LLM arms are not deterministic and have no seed to fix. No reference pack sets a temperature, the LLM settings note that one supported model rejects sampling parameters, and provider-side models change behind alias names such as the ones recorded today. Even the offline arm is not byte-identical in the current format (random id, wall-clock time, measured latency). As written the test can pass only for the offline arm, or for remote arms by replaying stored responses, which checks the statistics and not the model.

- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:86-87 - 'Claude Sonnet 5 rejects sampling parameters'; temperature optional
- $ grep -n temperature packs/*/pack.yaml -> no match
- $ scratch rerun.py -> 'byte-identical re-run: False'; differing keys [id, latency_ms]
- $ scratch scan.py -> recorded remote models 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5', 'anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5', 'openai/gpt-oss-120b', 'jev-1.13.0'

**Proposed correction.** Define reproducibility in two layers. Layer 1 (all arms): every run stores a content-addressed per-case ledger; metrics, intervals and tests recomputed from the same ledger and seeds must be byte-identical. Layer 2 (remote arms): run K replicates (3 to 5), report the between-run spread and the case flip rate, and fold run-to-run variance into intervals with a two-level bootstrap (resample runs, then cases). Record the provider-reported model per call, require dated snapshots where offered, and detect silent drift with a small scheduled canary set.

### D149 (A9)

**The plan says.** Calibration: ECE with 10 equal-mass bins, with a percentile bootstrap interval (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** Binned ECE is biased upward at small n, and the percentile bootstrap inherits the bias. A perfectly calibrated model (true ECE 0) scores a mean equal-mass ECE of about 0.11-0.18 at n=30, 0.06-0.10 at n=100 and 0.03-0.04 at n=600, depending on the confidence distribution. Equal-mass bins are not well defined when confidences tie, and rule-based arms emit few distinct values: ai-guard has 10 distinct confidences in 600 cases with one tie group of 254 (a decile is 60), so 'deciles' are arbitrary cuts through tie groups; on this data the value moved only from 0.2109 to 0.2151 under a worst-case tie order and not at all under 200 random orders, so the effect is real but small here. The choice of binning can matter far more (inbox: 0.0051 equal-width vs 0.0009 equal-mass). The change also conflicts with code: the benchmark's equal-width bins feed the card's reliability table, the share filter and the drift monitor, which places each bin by its lower edge in tenths. The plan does not say which confidence is scored for multi-question packs (the primary is often derived), nor how abstentions and provider failures enter: today failures are dropped from calibration but counted wrong in accuracy, so arms are scored on different case sets. ECE is not a proper scoring rule.

- $ scratch stats.py (seed 0, 2,000 simulations) -> 'uniform(0.5,1): n=30: 0.183; n=100: 0.099; n=600: 0.041'; 'skewed high-confidence: n=30: 0.110; n=100: 0.062; n=600: 0.025'
- $ scratch conf2.py -> ai-guard test: 10 distinct confidences, largest tie group 254; equal-mass ECE {'file order': 0.2109, 'ties correct first': 0.2151, 'ties wrong first': 0.2109}; 200 random tie orders min 0.2109 max 0.2109
- $ scratch conf.py -> inbox test: equal-width (code) 0.0051; equal-mass 0.0009
- src/mendari/evals/monitoring.py:152-157 - PSI maps benchmark bins by round(low*10)
- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:131-135 - calibration over answered cases only

**Proposed correction.** Use a proper scoring rule as the calibration number for comparison: the Brier score (with its Murphy reliability and resolution decomposition) or log loss, with a paired bootstrap. Keep ECE as a description only: a debiased estimator (Kumar, Liang and Ma 2019), ties never split across bins, a minimum bin size, and 'not estimable' on small sets. Add it as a new field and leave the equal-width `bins` table as it is. Specify top-label ECE per question, and score every case in every arm (a failure counts as wrong at the confidence the system would have acted on).

### D150 (A9)

**The plan says.** False-automation rate is a per-arm metric and ranking criterion 2, compared between arms with exact McNemar (p17-18).

**Why it is wrong.** The plan never defines the denominator. The code divides wrong AUTO decisions by AUTO decisions that have a primary label: that value is undefined when nothing is automated (4 of 5 reference benchmarks; 123 of 166 shipped leaderboard rows), can be lowered by automating more easy cases, and cannot be compared with McNemar because each arm automates a different set of cases. It also misses the harm that matters most: on the inbox held-out set the offline configuration automated 7 emergencies it failed to flag, and its false-automation rate is 0.0% because the routing label matched.

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:143-148,226-227 - rate = wrong AUTO / AUTO with a primary label; share = wrong AUTO / all results
- $ scratch rerun.py -> critical detected 4/20, auto_missed 7; automation n 7, false_automation_rate 0.0
- $ scratch bench.py -> automation n 0 and false_automation_rate None in ai-guard, trial, prior-auth and referral benchmark.json; $ scratch count -> rate not null in 43 of 166 leaderboard rows

**Proposed correction.** Define three figures. (1) False automation = wrong AUTO / all labelled cases: a paired per-case indicator with a Clopper-Pearson interval and McNemar across arms; this is the ranking criterion (the report's existing false_automation_share is close to it). (2) AUTO error rate = wrong AUTO / AUTO, reported with its n and interval, 'not applicable' when policy forbids AUTO. (3) Automated critical cases = critical positives with outcome AUTO regardless of the recommendation: a zero-tolerance gate that fails the grade, as the pack merge gate already does. Add risk-coverage curves from the existing threshold sweep for comparison at matched automation rates.

### D151 (A9)

**The plan says.** Ranking order: 1. Critical-label recall ... 3. Accuracy 4. Calibration 5. Cost 6. Latency (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** Several criteria are not well-defined numbers. Criterion 1 is one number per critical label and the plan does not say how labels combine; component labels also overlap with decision labels: the default ai-guard configuration blocks 164 of 164 unsafe drafts while its component critical label unsafe_advice shows 102 of 164, because another slot catches the rest, so a worst-label rule would rank a configuration that blocks everything at 62%. 'Calibration' is two numbers (ECE and Brier) with no rule for which decides. Cost has no defined source: Jev's price is a field a pack variant can set, an LLM's cost is what the gateway reports, a local model reports none. Latency is wall-clock time from whichever machine ran the report. Ranking calibration ahead of cost also penalises conservative arms: ai-guard is 97.7% accurate with ECE 0.21 because 254 correct cases sit at 0.58 confidence, the safe direction, yet it would lose to any costlier arm with a smaller ECE.

- $ scratch bench.py -> ai-guard benchmark: critical ('verdict','block',164,164), ('unsafe_advice','yes',164,102), ('dose_exceeds_limit','yes',62,62); acc 0.9767, ece 0.2109, bins (0.5, 0.6, 254)
- $ scratch conf2.py -> ai-guard confidence 0.580122: (254 cases, 254 correct)
- src/mendari/providers/jev.py:69,160 and src/mendari/providers/llm.py:349-350 - cost sources
- src/mendari/evals/leaderboard.py:3-5 - rows come from local runs or a deployment's endpoint
- src/mendari/dashboard/leaderboard.js:14 - today's code uses the minimum across critical labels

**Proposed correction.** Define criterion 1 on the pack's decision-level critical outcome (was the case kept from automation and flagged), using the worst label's lower bound (maximin), and report component labels as diagnostics. Make calibration a pass/fail gate (bootstrap upper bound of the Brier reliability term within a tolerance) instead of a rank criterion. Compute cost from tokens and a dated public price table. After the safety gates and bands, present cost against safety and accuracy as a Pareto front (the dashboard already draws cost against accuracy). Leave latency unranked, or measure it on one fixed runner with repeated runs.

### D152 (A9)

**The plan says.** Each published result is signed with the existing Ed25519 tooling and is immutable; developers may request one re-run per version; results are re-run monthly (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** The existing tooling signs pack archives with the publisher's key. Reusing it would have the pack author sign their own grade. 'Immutable' also conflicts with re-runs and monthly refreshes unless results are appended and linked; the current leaderboard code replaces rows in place.

- src/mendari/hub/archive.py:130-148 - signature by the publisher key over the archive manifest
- src/mendari/evals/leaderboard.py:83-92 - a new report replaces the row

**Proposed correction.** Sign results with a separate Mendari grading key (key id, rotation and revocation published), over canonical JSON of the deterministic result body. Store results append-only by content hash with a 'supersedes' link; 'stale' and 'superseded' are states of old results, never edits.

### D153 (A9)

**The plan says.** Fixture tests check every interval, test and adjustment against reference values computed independently (scipy and statsmodels) (p19); ECE and Brier get percentile bootstrap intervals (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** Neither library is a dependency or installed today. More important, a seeded percentile bootstrap has no independent reference that matches value for value: scipy.stats.bootstrap draws from a NumPy generator, so its resamples differ from any standard-library implementation. The criterion is checkable for Clopper-Pearson, McNemar and Holm but not, as written, for the bootstrap intervals. The percentile method itself is weak where A9 needs it most: it is degenerate at the boundary and inherits the bias of binned ECE on small sets.

- pyproject.toml:37-47 - dev dependencies
- $ scratch bench.py -> scipy installed: False; statsmodels installed: False; numpy installed: False

**Proposed correction.** Exact methods: match scipy and statsmodels to 1e-12. Bootstrap: test the resampling engine by feeding both implementations the same index matrix (exact match), test end to end against scipy with a large resample count and a stated tolerance, and add analytic cases with known answers. Prefer a BCa or studentized bootstrap for Brier, and do not publish a bootstrap interval for ECE below the minimum set size.

### D154 (A9)

**The plan says.** Early scoreboards gate stage 3; rank only on frozen hidden sets; publish only with 100 positives per critical label; hidden sets frozen is a stage 3 exit gate (p1, p4, p5, p17-18).

**Why it is wrong.** Internally inconsistent as sequenced. The run order puts A9 before stage 3, but frozen sets with 100 positives are only required to exist by the end of stage 3. By A9's own rules every scoreboard before then must say 'insufficient evidence' and show no rank. The plan never says so, which invites showing ranked early scoreboards on today's 24-30 case in-repo holdouts.

### D155 (A9)

**The plan says.** Goal: a reproducible, model-agnostic scoreboard and grade for every pack; 'a grade is published only when ...'; 'never blend into one score' (p17-18).

**Why it is wrong.** A9 never defines what a grade is. The method ranks the four arms of one pack against each other; it does not say what is attached to the pack (a letter, a pass or fail, a rank among packs), and a single blended score is forbidden. The proprietary asset on p1 is 'the right to display a verified Mendari grade', so the most valuable output of this unit has no definition, and an arm ranking by itself says which provider mix is best for a pack, not whether the pack is good enough.

**Proposed correction.** Define the grade as a small set of scoped, pre-registered attestations per arm, each met, not met or insufficient evidence: for example 'no critical case automated', 'each critical label: recall at least 0.95 with 95% confidence on set X version N', 'false automation at most 1% with 95% confidence'. No letter and no composite. The arm ranking is a separate table under the grade.

### D156 (A9)

**The plan says.** Freshness: re-run when a provider reports a new model version, and monthly. Mark results stale after 30 days or on a version change (p18).

**Why it is wrong.** The plan gives the re-runs no budget or runner. Evaluations on a deployment spend that deployment's daily provider budgets and are capped at 200 cases per call. Today's boards run 6 LLM-arm configurations per dataset; on two graded sets of only 300 cases each that is 3,600 LLM-arm decisions per pack and 18,000 for five packs per monthly run, before any developer submission, against the owner's stated public-launch limit of 200 LLM calls a day (about 6,000 a month; stated outside the repository). A monthly cadence also collides with a 30-day limit: results go stale for a day or more in every 31-day month. For LLM arms each re-run is a new random draw, so a monthly refresh can flip ranks without any real change.

- src/mendari/core/decision.py:162-165 - for_evaluation(): evaluations spend the deployment's daily provider budgets
- src/mendari/server/app.py:259,875-876 - 200-case cap per remote evaluation
- $ scratch scan.py -> 6 '+llm' rows and 1-2 '+jev' rows per dataset
- owner's stated launch limits (session memory dated 2026-10-02, not in the repository): Jev 2,000 and LLM 200 calls a day

**Proposed correction.** Give the grading service its own provider budget and runner, sized from the set sizes and arm count in the method. Re-run an arm only when its pack digest, set or effective model changes or a canary set shows drift; otherwise extend validity. Set staleness at 45 days if the cadence is monthly. Pool replicate runs of remote arms so a refresh changes a rank only when the pooled evidence does.

### D157 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 2: per-user tokens 'replacing admin-only publishing'.

**Why it is wrong.** Publishing is not admin-only today. Namespace-bound publisher tokens already exist and are enforced; what is admin-only is creating a namespace and issuing a token. A build session told to 'replace admin-only publishing' would look for something that is not there and could miss what is actually wrong: no per-user identity, no revocation or expiry, a token that alone can register a new signing key, and an admin token that can add its own key and publish anywhere.

- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:510-515 - require_publisher accepts the namespace's token
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:526-542 - namespace creation and token issue are the admin-only routes
- tests/test_registry.py::test_publishing_needs_the_namespaces_token
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s1.py -> 'token alone registers a brand-new key: 201', 'admin publishes with it: 201'

**Proposed correction.** Reword: 'Publisher tokens become per user, self-service after a namespace claim, revocable and expiring; adding a signing key needs a signed-in session; the admin credential loses the ability to publish or register keys and keeps only review actions.'

### D158 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 1: the registry 'recomputes ... risk level from the pack itself'.

**Why it is wrong.** A risk level cannot be recomputed: it is the author's own declaration in pack.yaml, and the registry already shows that value. The reproduced bug is a card that disagrees with the manifest. The real exposure is untouched by this step: a publisher simply declares risk 0 or 1 and the pack automates wherever it is pulled.

- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:383 - risk already read from the manifest
- src/mendari/core/policy.py:154-156 - the AUTO cap trusts manifest.risk.level
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s3.py -> a community copy declaring risk 0 returned AUTO on 284 of 300 cases after pull

**Proposed correction.** Split it: (a) the card is rendered by the registry from the manifest; (b) the declared risk level is confirmed by a reviewer in the first-publish queue and stored as a registry field the publisher cannot change; (c) packs pulled from a registry are capped at HUMAN_REVIEW unless the deploying organization approves that digest.

### D159 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 1: cards and benchmarks recomputed 'from the pack itself'.

**Why it is wrong.** 'The pack itself' includes the uploader's evidence files. A pack archive carries evals/benchmark.json, evals/leaderboard.json and DECISION_CARD.md, all outside the pack digest, and the engine's card generator reads the first two and prints the pack's self-claimed publisher. A card recomputed 'from the pack itself' with the existing function therefore still shows forged figures and a false publisher, and would pass a test that only checks the risk row.

- src/mendari/core/pack.py:29-30 - evals/ and DECISION_CARD.md excluded from the digest
- src/mendari/core/card.py:60-61,66-67 - render_card reads the benchmark and leaderboard attestations and prints the manifest's publisher
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s2.py -> render_card on forged attestations: 112 of 395 lines differ, including '`verdict` accuracy | 100.0%' and 'n=1000000'
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s4.py -> 'published by Mayo Clinic (institutional)' for a community namespace

**Proposed correction.** Say which inputs are allowed: 'The card is rendered from the digested files only (manifest, policy, schema, changelog). Validation figures on the card come only from an evaluation the registry ran; the publisher line comes from the namespace record. evals/ and DECISION_CARD.md in an upload are never displayed.'

### D160 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 1: benchmarks recomputed 'from the pack itself and its public test sets'.

**Why it is wrong.** Two problems. First, a benchmark recomputed on the publisher's own test set is still publisher-chosen evidence (they pick the cases), so showing it as the pack's benchmark keeps the credibility gap A9 is meant to close. Second, recomputing means running an outside author's pack inside the registry at publish time. The repository's own security notes say pack patterns run with no time limit and promise outside packs an isolated process once a public registry exists; the plan's A3 and A10 ask for neither isolation nor an asynchronous job.

- README.md:568-572 and SECURITY.md:216-219 - lead: patterns on re with no time limit; 'an isolated process with memory and time limits' promised once uploads or a public registry exist
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:218-227 - publish already loads the pack in the registry process; :556-565 on the event loop
- .github/workflows/packs.yml:43-54 - the pull-request route already validates, tests, cards and evaluates a changed pack, in a CI runner
- plan p17-18 - A9: template-set scores shown separately, labelled 'regression check, not a ranking'

**Proposed correction.** State that the recomputed figure is labelled 'publisher's own test set: regression check, not a ranking', that only A9 hidden-set results may be called a grade, and that the re-run happens in an isolated job with memory and time limits, asynchronously, with the version shown as 'checks pending' until it finishes.

### D161 (A10)

**The plan says.** Acceptance: 'security headers pass a scanner check in CI'.

**Why it is wrong.** A green scanner does not prove the three named headers. The gate fails only on medium or high alerts; the scan runs over plain HTTP on localhost, where HSTS cannot be judged (the engine itself withholds HSTS on a local host); and the existing job is an OpenAPI scan of the engine, which does not load the Hub's pages. Which ZAP rules would fire on the registry and Hub was not run, so that part is inference.

- .github/workflows/ci.yml:383 - zap-api-scan.py against http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json
- scripts/zap_check.py:26 - only risk >= 2 blocks
- src/mendari/server/app.py:1509-1510 - HSTS is set only when the host is not local

**Proposed correction.** Acceptance: explicit tests assert the exact CSP, HSTS and frame-ancestors values on every registry route and every Hub page, and a ZAP baseline scan of the Hub plus an API scan of the registry report no medium or high alert.

### D162 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 3: 'audit-chained publish, yank and delete events'.

**Why it is wrong.** It reads as if yank and delete exist and only need an audit trail. Neither exists, and the plan never defines them. It also leaves out the other events a trusted registry needs chained (token issue and revoke, key add and revoke, publisher-type change, review decisions), and there is no token or key revocation at all.

- $ <skeptic>/run.py s1.py -> route list has no DELETE or yank route; 'DELETE version: 405 | POST yank: 404 | DELETE key: 404 | DELETE tokens: 405 | DELETE namespace: 405'

**Proposed correction.** Add a numbered step that defines yank (hidden from latest and search, still fetchable by exact version with a reason, version number never reusable), admin delete for legal or patient-data takedown with a tombstone, token and key revocation, and the client behaviour for a yanked cached pack; then chain all of these events.

### D163 (A10)

**The plan says.** Goal: 'nothing on a pack's page comes from the uploader unchecked', delivered by items 1-4.

**Why it is wrong.** The items cover the card, the benchmark and the risk level only. The page also shows the uploader's leaderboard file and site reports that any token holder can post under any site name. Signed site results are A11, which gates stage 6, so from stage 4 to stage 6 the public pack page would carry spoofable 'site evidence'.

- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:401 - leaderboard stored as the pack carries it
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:609-618 - any publisher token may submit a report under any site name
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s1.py -> "sites: [('Mayo Clinic', 'mendari', 1.0, 600), ('Cleveland Clinic', 'newcomer', 1.0, 600)]"

### D164 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 5 and the 1-2 week estimate: deploy 'with the same sign-in and organizations as the platform'.

**Why it is wrong.** The registry and Hub share nothing with the platform's sign-in today: the registry has its own bearer tokens and tables, the Hub has no sign-in, and the only deploy config excludes the Hub. The plan does not say whether the registry is mounted in the engine app (one origin and cookie) or runs as its own project on a subdomain, which decides cookie scope, CSP, limits and database. With 0 of 14 items done and items 2 and 5 both waiting on A6, 1-2 weeks for all of A10 looks low; the size of the gap is evidence, the estimate is judgement.

- vercel.json:8-12 - only app.py deployed; hub/** excluded
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:502-515 - registry auth is its own bearer-token check
- hub/lib/registry.ts:77-87 - the Hub calls the registry with no credentials

**Proposed correction.** Add a decision before the build: same-origin mount or separate project, and which database. Split the prompt: A10a (card and labels, headers, limits, chain, yank, revocation, tables, pull-side cap; buildable now) and A10b (accounts, claims, review queue, deploy; after A6), and estimate each.

### D165 (A10)

**The plan says.** Item 1: 'Today a risk-2 pack was published with a card saying risk 1'.

**Why it is wrong.** Read literally, it suggests a shipped or published pack is in that state. At the audited commit every shipped card equals a fresh render and matches its pack.yaml, and the risk rows also matched at the plan's own commit. The statement is true only as 'the registry accepts such a pack', which was reproduced.

- $ <skeptic>/run.py s2.py -> all five packs: 'shipped == render_card: True'
- $ git show 0182417c:packs/<pack>/DECISION_CARD.md | grep 'Risk level' -> matches pack.yaml for all five packs

### D166 (A10)

**The plan says.** Acceptance: 'an unclaimed namespace can't be published to'.

**Why it is wrong.** This already passes at the audited commit (403 for a publisher token or no token, 404 for the admin token), so it cannot show that item 2 was built. It says nothing about the cases item 2 creates: a namespace claimed by someone else, a namespace still in the review queue, a revoked token, or the admin credential.

### D167 (A10)

**The plan says.** A10 as a whole: 'anyone can publish and pull community packs', with requirements only on the registry and the page.

**Why it is wrong.** The prompt has no requirement for the pulling side, which is where a pack reaches a decision. Today the client trusts whatever key the registry lists on first contact, accepts a plain-http registry, has no revocation, lets a pulled pack replace a bundled pack of the same id, and lets a pulled pack automate on its self-declared risk level. A registry that passes every A10 acceptance test would still deliver packs to clients this way.

- src/mendari/hub/client.py:232-243 - keys are trusted because the registry listed them, pinned on first use
- $ <skeptic>/run.py s3.py -> 'pull over http://registry.example.org succeeded'; 'after pull resolves to cache copy (same version): True'; outcomes of a pulled community pack: AUTO 284 of 300
- src/mendari/core/policy.py:154-156 - no origin input to the AUTO cap

**Proposed correction.** Add an item 'Client trust': a registry key shipped with the client counter-signs accepted versions; HTTPS required except localhost; key and version revocation checked on pull and at server start; bundled ids cannot be replaced by a pulled pack; a pack whose origin is a registry is capped at HUMAN_REVIEW unless the deploying organization approves its digest. Acceptance tests for each.

### D168 (A11)

**The plan says.** The payload includes 'a dataset hash' (p.20, item 2)

**Why it is wrong.** An unkeyed hash of the site's file is a confirmation and membership oracle: anyone holding a candidate file (or, for a small low-entropy set, able to enumerate candidates) can test whether it is the site's data, and the same hash links a site's submissions across registries. It also proves nothing to the receiver, who cannot see the data. The code already takes the stricter position: it strips the dataset name and SHA-256 and a test asserts it, so the plan is weaker than the code, and a build session following the plan would have to delete that assertion against the shared header's rule not to weaken an existing check (p.6).

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:89 - sha256 over the raw file bytes
- src/mendari/evals/share.py:42 - dataset reduced to n; tests/test_share.py:20 - '# no name, no digest'

**Proposed correction.** Send a keyed commitment instead: HMAC-SHA-256 of the file under a secret the site keeps and never shares. It lets the registry detect an identical re-submission from the same site and lets the site later prove to an auditor which file it used, without giving outsiders an oracle. State that the commitment is not evidence of data quality.

### D169 (A11)

**The plan says.** A11 has no rule about repeated shares from the same site

**Why it is wrong.** Two metrics-only payloads that differ by one case disclose that case. Reproduced: sharing the first 399 and then all 400 records of the same file differs in exactly the cells (destination: billing->billing, urgency: routine->routine) and AUTO +1, which are the 400th record's true labels, prediction and outcome. Cell suppression does not prevent this because the large cells move. --limit makes it trivial and the registry accepts every submission.

- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> 'n-1 vs n differ in: [(destination, billing, billing, 1), (urgency, routine, routine, 1)] | last record labels: {destination: billing, urgency: routine}'; 'outcome delta: {AUTO: 1, HUMAN_REVIEW: 0, ABSTAIN: 0, BLOCK: 0}'
- src/mendari/cli.py:140-141 and :162-165 - --limit and --share combine freely
- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> '2d identical body twice -> HTTP 201, 201'

**Proposed correction.** Add to A11: one live submission per (site, pack digest, configuration, dataset commitment); a new submission replaces the old one rather than sitting beside it; the registry refuses a submission whose n differs from the same site's previous one for that pack by less than the suppression threshold; --share refuses a --limit run. Keep superseded submissions out of every public answer.

### D170 (A11)

**The plan says.** 'Suppress any cell under 10 (the existing default) before sending' (p.20, item 3)

**Why it is wrong.** Four problems. (a) The existing default covers only subgroup cells and calibration bins, so this is new work, not a default. (b) Primary suppression alone is undone by totals: dataset n is sent, so the suppressed subgroup cells' total is derivable (101 on the example file) and a lone suppressed cell exactly; a dropped calibration bin's size and error mass come back from the ECE that is still sent (2 cases and 0.9003 recovered exactly). (c) It contradicts item 4 and the purpose of the network: for a good pack the missed-critical-case count is almost always under 10, so the false-negative counts that pooled sensitivity needs would be suppressed, and treating them as zero biases the pooled result upward. (d) It does not say whether zero counts are suppressed, and '0 missed' is the most important number. It also conflicts with item 2: calibration bins are to be sent, yet dropping bins under 10 leaves bins that no longer reproduce the reported ECE.

- src/mendari/evals/share.py:38-47 - only bins and subgroup cells are filtered
- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> 'subgroup topic: ... recoverable total from payload = dataset n - sent = 101'; 'calibration urgency: ... recovered dropped n=2, recovered mass=0.9003 actual=0.9003'
- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> a 20-positive site run: detected 4, missed 16, auto_missed 7 (the auto-missed count is under 10); $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/referral.py -> referral example, 41 and 51 positives, 0 missed (every false-negative cell here is zero or under 10)

**Proposed correction.** Split the rule. Apply the threshold, with complementary suppression and a minimum dataset size, to cells that describe people: subgroup membership and anything cross-tabulated by a demographic or site attribute. For the pre-registered safety endpoints (TP, FN and auto-missed per critical label over the whole dataset) send exact counts whenever the denominator meets a minimum (for example 20 positives), under the site agreement in Part B. Say that zeros are sent. Require that no suppressed value be derivable from any total in the payload, and test that.

### D171 (A11)

**The plan says.** 'A pooled result from summed counts with Clopper-Pearson intervals' (p.20, item 4)

**Why it is wrong.** Summing counts assumes every site draws from one population. When case mix differs, the pooled figure can reverse the per-site ordering (Simpson's paradox), and the exact binomial interval is too narrow because it ignores between-site variance. Worked example, recomputed: pack A detects 90/100 and 10/50 at two sites (pooled 66.7%, CP 58.5-74.1%); pack B detects 19/20 and 60/200 (pooled 35.9%, CP 29.6-42.6%). B is better at both sites and looks far worse pooled, with intervals that do not overlap.

- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/stats.py (pure-Python Clopper-Pearson by bisection) -> 'Simpson A: 0.9 0.2 pooled 0.667 (0.5852, 0.7414)'; 'Simpson B: 0.95 0.3 pooled 0.359 (0.2957, 0.4263)'

**Proposed correction.** Lead with per-site estimates and exact intervals. Give the summed-count Clopper-Pearson figure only with the label 'fixed-effect, assumes sites are alike', and withhold it when the homogeneity check fails. Add a random-effects summary (beta-binomial or logit-normal) with a prediction interval for a new site once there are at least five sites. Never compare two packs on pooled site figures unless both were evaluated at the same sites.

### D172 (A11)

**The plan says.** 'Chi-square test of homogeneity, alpha 0.05' (p.20, item 4)

**Why it is wrong.** The chi-square approximation needs expected counts of about 5 or more per cell. Misses are rare by design, so expected miss counts will be far below that at most sites: three sites with 0/18, 1/12 and 3/15 misses give expected miss counts of 1.6, 1.07 and 1.33. In that example the approximate and exact p-values happen to be close (0.132 against 0.118), so the larger problem is power: a 0% against 20% miss rate raises no warning under either test, and 'no warning' would read as 'sites agree' when it only means 'cannot tell'. One alpha of 0.05 applied to every metric, label, configuration and pack will also raise false warnings routinely.

- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/stats.py -> 'chi-square: expected misses [1.6, 1.07, 1.33] chi2 4.047 df 2 critical 5.991; p = 0.1322'; 'exact (Fisher-Freeman-Halton) p = 0.1184'

**Proposed correction.** Use an exact test of homogeneity (Fisher-Freeman-Halton) or a seeded Monte Carlo permutation test whenever any expected count is under 5; restrict testing to the pre-registered primary endpoints; show an explicit 'too few sites or cases to assess agreement' state; report the between-site spread (range and a heterogeneity estimate) alongside the test rather than a bare warning.

### D173 (A11)

**The plan says.** Sites 'share metrics' with `mendari eval --share` when they choose to (p.20, goal and item 2)

**Why it is wrong.** Sharing is opt-in per run, after the site has seen the result. A site, or a vendor working with it, can run many datasets, thresholds or configurations and share only the flattering one. The network then measures willingness to publish. Nothing in A11 or Part B counters this.

- src/mendari/cli.py:143 and :162-165 - the report is computed locally first; --share is an optional flag on the same command
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:605-618 - the registry learns of an evaluation only when a report is posted

**Proposed correction.** Add pre-registration: before running, the site requests an evaluation ticket from the registry bound to (site, pack digest, configuration, dataset commitment). The payload must carry the ticket. The Hub shows 'k of m registered evaluations reported' per pack, and the pilot agreement commits sites to report every registered run.

### D174 (A11)

**The plan says.** A site signature makes shared results trustworthy (p.20, item 1 and acceptance)

**Why it is wrong.** A signature proves who sent the numbers, not that the claimed pack digest and configuration produced them, nor that they were not typed by hand. Today the receiver does not even compare the reported digest with the published one, and stores rates without checking them against counts (accuracy 1.0 with n = 1e9 was accepted). The plan also omits replay protection, key rotation and revocation, and who verifies that a key belongs to the named health system.

- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:299-301 - only id and version are compared
- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> '2f wrong digest, accuracy 1.0, n=1e9 -> HTTP 201 n=1000000000 accuracy=1.0'

**Proposed correction.** Add to A11: reject a digest that is not the published version's; accept counts only and recompute every rate; bind each submission to a registry nonce; add key rotation and revocation; add proof of execution, for example the registry sends a small set of public synthetic canary cases with the ticket and the site returns a hash over the engine's decisions on them, which only the pack with that digest and configuration produces. Label site evidence 'self-reported, signed by the site' everywhere, and add the site identity check as an owner item in Part B.

### D175 (A11)

**The plan says.** Acceptance: 'a payload containing any case text fails validation on both sides'

**Why it is wrong.** No validator can recognise 'case text' in general, so the criterion is untestable as written unless the schema has no free string anywhere. Several fields are strings by nature: label names, subgroup attribute names and values, provider model ids, the site name. Today subgroup values come straight from the site's file and a pack declares attribute names only.

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:276 - subgroup value = str(record['attributes'][attribute]); src/mendari/core/spec.py:403 - subgroups: list[str]
- $ python scratchpad/tmp/A11-skeptic/verify.py -> subgroup values sent are whatever the site's file holds (here en, unknown, control)

**Proposed correction.** Restate as: every string in the payload is either an enumerated value taken from the published pack (question names, labels, declared subgroup attributes and their declared values) or matches a fixed pattern (hex digest, semantic version, model id); anything else is rejected on both sides. Packs declare the allowed values of each subgroup attribute; other values are counted under 'other'.

### D176 (A11)

**The plan says.** Aggregation and display are described per pack (items 4 and 5)

**Why it is wrong.** The plan's own principle is that every pack is scored in four configurations (p.2). A11 never says site results are stratified by configuration, and pooling a rules-only site with a Jev + LLM site is meaningless. The current summary rows do not carry the configuration. The plan also forbids free text but asks for 'real-world evidence' without any description of the reference standard (who labelled, how, over what period), which is what makes chart-reviewed results interpretable.

- launch-plan p.2 - 'Every pack is scored in four configurations'

**Proposed correction.** Key every site result, pooled figure, range, site count and homogeneity test by (pack digest, configuration). Add a small closed vocabulary to the payload for the reference standard: labelling method, number of reviewers, adjudication yes or no, sampling (consecutive, random, enriched), and data period as year-quarter.

### D177 (A11)

**The plan says.** Sites evaluate 'inside their environment, and share metrics only' (p.20 goal) while every pack is scored in four configurations including + Jev and + LLM (p.2)

**Why it is wrong.** Three of the four configurations use providers the code marks as remote. A site that evaluates them on chart-reviewed data sends the pack's declared input fields for every case to Jev or an LLM gateway, so the evaluation is not inside the site's environment. ### D178 (A11)

**The plan says.** A11 gates only stage 6 and has no 'Requires' line (p.5 table, p.20)

**Why it is wrong.** `mendari eval --share`, the receiving endpoint and the Hub 'Site reports' table already ship, and the docs already promise 'no cases, ids or small groups'. Alternatively disable --share and the reports routes until A11 is built. Add 'Requires A6, A9 and A10' to A11.

### D179 (A12)

**The plan says.** p2-p3 and p21: 'EHR readiness 2.5 of 5' per 'your own launch-readiness report and EHR scorecard', and the A12 goal 'from 2.5 to a credible 3 of 5'

### D180 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 1: 'Open mode stays unauthenticated only for local sandboxes'

### D181 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 1: 'add CORS for registered EHR origins'

**Why it is wrong.** Unscoped, it collides with an existing safety invariant: the origin guard lets requests with an Authorization header skip the cross-site check because Mendari never grants a CORS preflight, and the shared header forbids weakening a safety rule. EHR backends call CDS services server to server and do not need CORS; only browser-based clients do.

- src/mendari/server/origin.py:22-24 and :65-68
- src/mendari/standards/capability.py:203 - cors False, asserted at tests/test_backend_services.py:237

**Proposed correction.** Limit CORS to /cds-services and /cds-services/* for registered origins, headers Authorization and Content-Type only, no Allow-Credentials, never on a cookie-authenticated route; state that the FHIR base stays cors:false.

### D182 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 1: verify 'against that EHR's registered JWKS (iss, aud, exp, jti replay check)'

**Why it is wrong.** It omits what a registration must pin for this to be safe: the request's fhirServer (otherwise a registered EHR's token could direct Mendari to read from another allow-listed server), the JWT header's jku (a caller-chosen key URL must never be followed), what aud must equal, and iat with a maximum lifetime. It also does not mention that today's bearer parser caps credentials at 512 characters, which a real signed JWT exceeds.

- src/mendari/standards/cds_hooks.py:135-147 - fhirServer is taken from the request and checked only against the global allow-list
- src/mendari/server/backend_services.py:77 - the existing verifier refuses jku outright; :360 - a maximum lifetime is enforced there
- src/mendari/server/auth.py:334 - 512-character cap; $ probe4.py -> a 768-character JWT is refused as malformed

**Proposed correction.** Add: a registration binds iss to keys (or one pinned jwks_uri), an organization and allowed fhirServer bases; jku is accepted only if equal to the registered URL; aud must equal the public URL of the service or discovery endpoint called; iat and a maximum lifetime are checked; the JWT branch has its own size limit.

### D183 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 3: 'use MedicationRequest'

**Why it is wrong.** Clinically under-specified. The trial criteria ('stable metformin for 90 days', 'no insulin in the last 90 days') are computed from MedicationStatement start and end dates. A MedicationRequest is an order with authoredOn and a status, not a usage period, so a straight swap changes what the criteria mean. Today the gap fails in both directions, including the unsafe one.

- packs/clinical-trial-prescreener/fhir/mapping.yaml:46-58 - start and end from effectivePeriod
- $ probe2.py - the same metformin as a MedicationRequest turns a candidate into not_eligible with no card
- $ probe5.py - current insulin as a MedicationRequest leaves an ineligible patient a 'candidate' card

**Proposed correction.** Specify the derivation (authoredOn as earliest start, validityPeriod and status for stop, needs_review when the period cannot be established) and require clinician sign-off on it before the pack is rebuilt.

### D184 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 3: a failed fetch should 'degrade to ABSTAIN with a reason'

**Why it is wrong.** It covers only fetches that fail loudly. The more dangerous cases today fail silently: linked notes, MedicationRequest, non-first codings and search pages beyond the eleventh are dropped with no error, and the pack then decides on a partial record (a pregnant patient, a patient on insulin and a patient with a recent MI each get a 'possible candidate' card). It also misses a second loud path: one malformed resource anywhere in the chart fails the whole hook with 400. And it does not say whether an ABSTAIN shows a card, which matters for alert fatigue and for order hooks where silence can be read as 'no prior authorization needed'.

- $ probe2.py - note as attachment.url: not_eligible -> candidate, card shown
- $ probe5.py - insulin as MedicationRequest, and MI with a local coding first: candidate, card shown
- $ probe3.py - unknown element or empty string in one prefetched Observation -> HTTP 400; 12-page search -> 11 pages read, no marker
- src/mendari/standards/cds_hooks.py:104-106 - card suppression is per recommendation

**Proposed correction.** Add: 'data that is present but unreadable, unmapped, truncated or structurally rejected (a linked attachment, an unsupported resource type, no coding in a known system, more pages than were read, a resource the R4 gate refuses) is a recorded reason and forces HUMAN_REVIEW or ABSTAIN; it is never treated as absent and never fails the hook.' State the card behaviour for ABSTAIN per hook type.

### D185 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 3: 'accept the site's own note codes'

**Why it is wrong.** It does not say where the codes go. Today the only place is the pack's logic files, which are inside the pack digest, so a site that adds its codes runs a different pack from the one that was graded. That conflicts with the plan's own principle that a grade names the pack version it applies to (p2).

- packs/referral-router/logic/checklist.yaml:3-4 - 'A site adds the document codes it uses'
- packs/referral-router/pack.yaml:45-49 - 'Add a site's codes before use'
- src/mendari/core/pack.py:90-94 - a pack file is read as the bytes its digest covers

**Proposed correction.** Require a site code map outside the pack, hashed into every decision and eval report, so a grade reads 'pack X at version v with map M'.

### D186 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 5 and acceptance: 'the Inferno SMART App Launch and Bulk Data test kits ... Inferno kits pass'

**Why it is wrong.** Ambiguous about roles. Mendari is a SMART app (client) for EHR launch, a Backend Services token server for its own API, and a Bulk Data client; it has no authorization endpoint and serves no $export. Server-side suites of those kits have little or nothing to run against Mendari, so 'pass' is undefined. (Which client suites the current kit versions offer could not be checked offline; this part is from general knowledge.)

- src/mendari/server/backend_services.py:134-147 - smart-configuration: token_endpoint only, 'no authorization_endpoint'
- src/mendari/standards/bulk.py:1-16 - an export consumer
- src/mendari/standards/capability.py:49-58 - 'not a FHIR data server'

**Proposed correction.** Name the suites: a SMART App Launch client suite for the launched app, the Backend Services group for /auth/token, a Bulk client suite (or a second server implementation) for the exporter; pin kit versions by digest.

### D187 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 item 5: 'the HL7 validator with a terminology server' as a CI test

**Why it is wrong.** CI deliberately runs the validator with -tx n/a so merges do not depend on a remote service. Making a public terminology server a required check reintroduces that fragility, and the prior-auth pack's CPT codes may not validate on a public server (licensed content).

- scripts/fhir_validate.py:18-19, :43, :62
- packs/prior-auth-preflight/fhir/mapping.yaml:9 - CPT codes

**Proposed correction.** Keep the offline run as the required gate; add the terminology-backed run as a scheduled or non-required job with an explicit, reviewed list of expected findings.

### D188 (A12)

**The plan says.** p21 acceptance: 'every reference pack decides on the vendor's sandbox patients without a failed hook'

**Why it is wrong.** Not achievable as written for two of the five reference packs: ai-guard has no CDS service, and the inbox router's hook is a Mendari-specific type that no EHR fires. It also rewards the wrong thing: with today's mappings a hook can 'decide without failing' on a record it mostly could not read (the prior-auth pack answers not_checked, silently, for any payer it cannot name).

- $ probe.py hooks offered - four services, the inbox on 'mendari-message-received', none for ai-guard
- packs/patient-inbox-router/pack.yaml:217
- $ probe4.py - payor by reference -> not_checked, no card, no system action, HTTP 200

**Proposed correction.** Scope the criterion to the packs with standard hooks (patient-view, order-sign), say how the inbox pack is exercised (SMART launch or a worker), and add a data-coverage condition: for each patient, the fields each pack requires were found, or the decision abstained with a reason.

### D189 (A12)

**The plan says.** p5: A12 'EHR pilot readiness', rough effort 4-7 weeks

**Why it is wrong.** Likely understated (an estimate, not a measurement). Summing this audit's per-item estimates gives eight items of 1-2 weeks each (JWT trust, linked notes, code systems, MedicationRequest, site code map, the CDS client job, the Inferno SMART job, vendor fit) and about twelve of 1-3 days: roughly 10 to 20 engineer-weeks before any fitting to the vendor's sandbox data, which cannot start until the owner names the vendor.

- the effort fields of the items above
- $ git diff --stat 0182417c..HEAD (A12 paths) - no A12 work has landed since the plan was written

**Proposed correction.** Split A12 into a vendor-independent part that can start now (A12.1, A12.2, the generic halves of A12.3, A12.5a-d) and a vendor-fit part gated on the owner's choice, and re-estimate each.

### D190 (A13)

**The plan says.** A13.2: run the existing monitor on a cron and post alerts to the alert webhook (p.22).

**Why it is wrong.** The existing monitor is not fit to page on, in both directions. It compares observed accuracy on labelled decisions (in practice the reviewed, low-confidence subset) with the benchmark's accuracy over all cases, with no confidence interval and a floor of 20 cases. With the inbox pack's figures (benchmark 99.3%, tolerance 3%) a single disagreement in 20 to 27 labelled cases is a 'high' alert, and a week whose review overrides are at or even below the benchmark's own expected override rate raises one. It has no operational signals: a week in which every decision fails its providers raises nothing. Run without --org on a multi-organization database, one reviewer's single thumbs-down on an automated decision in any organization raises a 'high' alert for 7 days. The plan also never says where the webhook goes: no Part B item creates the receiver, and the alert body is Mendari's own shape.

- $ python tmp/A13-skeptic/p2/probe.py -> B healthy week (567 AUTO unlabelled; 31 reviewed, 3 overridden): observed_accuracy 0.9032 vs benchmark 0.9933, alerts [accuracy/high]; B3 31 reviewed, 2 overridden (6.5%, below the benchmark's expected 9.7%): observed 0.9355, alerts [accuracy]; B2 31 reviewed, none overridden: alerts []
- packs/patient-inbox-router/evals/benchmark.json - decisions.review: n 31, expected_override_rate 0.0968; questions.destination.accuracy 0.9933 over n 600; packs/patient-inbox-router/pack.yaml:209 - degradation_tolerance: 0.03
- src/mendari/evals/monitoring.py:81-91 - alert if observed < target - tolerance once labelled >= 20 (MIN_LABELLED, line 30); no interval. 19/20 = 0.950 and 26/27 = 0.963 are both below 0.9633
- src/mendari/evals/monitoring.py:118-121 - 'labelled' = decisions with a final label and a recommendation
- $ same script -> C outage week (200 decisions, all ABSTAIN, quota_exhausted): automated_rate 0.0, alerts []; src/mendari/core/audit.py:1673-1686 - decision_rows selects no error or failure column
- src/mendari/evals/monitoring.py:95-97 - any automated decision rated wrong in 7 days is a 'high' alert; src/mendari/cli.py:846-848 - without --org every organization's rows are pooled

**Proposed correction.** Reword A13.2: before scheduling, (a) compare like with like: the reviewed subset's override rate against the benchmark's decisions.review.expected_override_rate with a Wilson or exact binomial bound, and observed accuracy against the benchmark only where labels are sampled from all outcomes; (b) add operational alerts: share of decisions with provider errors, a jump in ABSTAIN or BLOCK, zero decisions, chain verify false, budget or quota above 80%; (c) run per organization; (d) name the alert destination and its format, with a daily heartbeat; (e) acceptance adds 'a healthy seeded week raises no alert' and 'a seeded provider outage raises one'.

### D191 (A13)

**The plan says.** A13.3: a single kill switch that forces HUMAN_REVIEW (p.22).

**Why it is wrong.** Underspecified in ways that matter for safety. 'Forces HUMAN_REVIEW' read literally would turn BLOCK (input rejected) and ABSTAIN (no recommendation) into reviews with recommendations they do not have; the code's own rule is that policy only lowers automation. It does not say the switch must take effect at once on every serverless instance (an environment variable would need a redeploy), who may flip it (operator or an organization's admin), that flipping is recorded in the audit chain, or that the emergency rule's priority must survive. The nearest existing mechanism shows the trap: a zero quota stops automation but downgrades an emergency from stat to routine.

- src/mendari/core/policy.py:1-9 and 103-106 - caps apply only to AUTO; ABSTAIN keeps no recommendation
- $ python tmp/A13-skeptic/p1/probe.py -> decisions=0: emergency outcome=ABSTAIN priority=routine (normally HUMAN_REVIEW, stat)
- src/mendari/server/vercel.py:55-61 - the app, and with it every setting, is built once at import on Vercel

**Proposed correction.** Specify: an 'automation hold' stored in the database, scoped to the deployment, an organization, a pack or a digest; it caps AUTO to HUMAN_REVIEW after the policy rules run and changes nothing else; effective on the next request on every instance; set and lifted by a named person with a reason, chained and logged; visible in health, the Decision Card and the dashboard; a CLI break-glass for when the API is down.

### D192 (A13)

**The plan says.** A13 gates stage 5 only (table p.5; gate figure p.4), so the kill switch, incident runbook and scheduled monitoring arrive just before self-service.

**Why it is wrong.** The kill switch is an engine safety control that every self-hosting site needs, not a hosted-operations feature. For a risk level 0-1 pack there is no approval to revoke, so until it exists the only ways to stop a misbehaving inbox router are to stop serving it (404) or to change settings and redeploy. Design partners at stage 2 are bound to synthetic data, but stage 3 makes the code public, where anyone may run it on real messages, and stage 4 runs outside authors' packs on Mendari's servers; both open before a kill switch, runbook, scheduled monitoring or status page is required. The repository already publishes response-time commitments in SECURITY.md with no incident procedure behind them.

- packs/patient-inbox-router/pack.yaml:13-14 - risk level 0; src/mendari/core/policy.py:154-156 - level <= 1 automates with no governance step
- $ python tmp/A13-skeptic/p1/probe.py -> MENDARI_PACKS without the pack: http 404 PackNotFoundError
- SECURITY.md:17 - acknowledge within 3 working days, fix critical issues within 14 days
- Plan p.11 (pilot agreement 'covering synthetic data only'), p.14 (stage 3: 'Anyone self-hosts'; stage 4: 'Build in the hosted pack store')

**Proposed correction.** Move the kill switch code and its end-to-end test into A4 (at the latest before the stage 3 gate). Make the incident runbook and scheduled monitoring a stage 4 gate at the latest, since that is when strangers' packs first run on the hosted site. Leave the status page, firewall enforcement and usage dashboards at stage 5.

### D193 (A13)

**The plan says.** A13.1 and its acceptance: a status page with uptime checks on the API, sign-in, decide, the registry and the Hub that reflects a simulated outage (p.22).

**Why it is wrong.** It assumes the service exposes something an uptime checker can use. The public health endpoint is deliberately static (a tested hardening decision), so it cannot reflect a database outage; sign-in is a redirect to an external identity provider that a checker cannot complete; decide needs a credential, and every check appends a decision to a permanent hash chain and spends an organization's quota; the Hub has no health route.

- src/mendari/core/decision.py:342-343 - every decision is recorded and chained

**Proposed correction.** Specify the checks: a new deep readiness route (cached, no secrets), the sign-in route followed to the identity provider's authorize URL, a synthetic decide by a dedicated status organization and narrow key (excluded from partner statistics and quotas), the registry's /v1/health, and the Hub's home page; the anonymous three-field health stays as it is.

### D194 (A13)

**The plan says.** A13.5: usage dashboards for Jev and LLM spend per organization, to check against the dollar caps the owner sets (p.22).

**Why it is wrong.** It presumes per-organization dollar accounting by provider exists to chart. Mendari's limits are call counts; per-organization Jev and LLM calls are counted only when a quota for that metric is set (the planned launch quota, decisions=5000, counts neither); a decision row stores one cost figure, not split by provider; a pack chooses the model and up to 32,000 output tokens per call, so calls do not map to dollars; LLM cost is recorded only when the gateway reports it and Jev cost is an estimate from a hard-coded list price; evaluation spend is saved in the report with its organization but charged to no organization's counter.

- src/mendari/core/audit.py:71-89 - decisions: one cost_usd column and org; no provider split

- src/mendari/server/app.py:868-873 - evaluations spend deployment budgets only; src/mendari/core/audit.py:605-617 - the report is saved with its organization
- docs/deploying-with-phi.md:603-605 - planned MENDARI_ORG_DAILY_LIMITS=decisions=5000 (a lead)

**Proposed correction.** Split item 5 in two: first a usage ledger (per day, organization, provider type and purpose: calls, tokens, cost with 'unknown' explicit, evaluations and guard included, written with or without quotas), then the dashboard and 80% alerts on top of it. **Proposed correction.** Define the four configurations as provider classes (deterministic only; + a specialised probabilistic model; + a general LLM; + both), declare them per pack in `evaluation.configurations`, say that each grade names the exact model, and state that the default model is a deployment setting with no engine default.

### D204 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** Header p.6 'real statistics'; Stage 3 gate (p.4): 'hidden sets frozen with 100+ positives per critical label'; p.3 'confidence intervals'.

**Why it is wrong.** The plan never names an interval method, a confidence level, a minimum n per claim or how configurations are compared, so 'real statistics' cannot be checked. 100 positives with zero misses supports only a one-sided 95% upper bound of about 3% on the miss rate (1 - 0.05^(1/100) = 0.0295), and a two-sided Wilson lower bound on detection of 96.3%; one miss in 100 gives a Wilson interval of 94.6% to 99.8%. The current regression gate compares point estimates with an epsilon of 1e-9, so it cannot tell noise from regression.

- src/mendari/evals/gate.py:19, :71
- $ python: 0 misses in n=100 -> one-sided 95% upper bound 0.0295, Wilson lower bound 0.963; 99/100 -> Wilson [0.9455, 0.9982]
- $ python: positives needed, zero misses, for a 95% lower bound of 97% -> Wilson 125, exact two-sided 122, exact one-sided 99; for 99% -> Wilson 381, exact two-sided 368, exact one-sided 299
- $ grep for wilson|bootstrap|interval functions in src -> none

**Proposed correction.** State in the header: proportions carry Wilson 95% intervals; differences between configurations use a paired, seeded bootstrap on the same records; every grade prints n and the interval; a critical-label claim of 'detects at least X%' needs the interval's lower bound above X. Then size the hidden sets from the claim: with zero misses, about 125 positives support 97% and about 380 support 99% (Wilson, two-sided); 100 positives support about 96%.

### D205 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** Shared header, p.6 (rules list) has no rule about the audit chain.

**Why it is wrong.** Seven of the thirteen prompts add state-changing routes (accounts, keys, pack upload, labelling, grading, registry, site evaluations). Without a rule, new writes can skip the chain, as evaluation reports and the whole registry already do, and the trust claim rests on tables that anyone with database access can edit undetected, including the governance approvals that unlock automation.

- src/mendari/core/audit.py:605-618 - save_report not chained
- src/mendari/hub/registry.py:146-306 - writes with no chain
- $ (scratch) chain probe: edited report and truncated tail both verify ok; governance probe: un-revoked and forged approvals are active and verify ok

**Proposed correction.** Add: 'Every new state-changing route or command appends a chained event (ids and hashes only, no free text) and is added to the route inventory test; anything deliberately unchained is listed there with the reason. State that unlocks automation or access is read from, or reconciled with, the chain.'

### D206 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** Shared header, p.6 has no rule about derived pack artifacts or grade freshness.

**Why it is wrong.** CLAUDE.md requires regenerating data, models, benchmark and card together when a pack changes, but the header (the only text pasted before each prompt) omits it, and CI does not catch a stale benchmark or card. A session that edits a rule or policy can ship a card whose figures belong to a different pack digest.

- .github/workflows/ci.yml:79
- $ (scratch) pack with a changed threshold: validate ok, card rendered the new digest with the old benchmark's figures
- CLAUDE.md ('Pack artifacts are derived')

**Proposed correction.** Add: 'If a pack, a generator or policy code changes, rerun scripts/build-reference-pack.sh and commit data, models, benchmark and card together; a benchmark or leaderboard row whose pack digest differs from the pack is a failure.'

### D207 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Synthetic data only. Never touch production or the hosted deployment.'

**Why it is wrong.** A session cannot obey the second sentence as written if the hosted project deploys from Git, which the repository's own configuration implies: Git deployments are disabled only for Dependabot branches, a workflow exists to clean up the database branch that every preview deployment creates, and migrations run at startup. So pushing a branch creates a hosted preview with a database branch, and merging to main redeploys production and migrates its database. (Whether the Vercel project is connected is a hosted setting I could not check.)

**Proposed correction.** 'Never call the hosted deployment or use production credentials. A merge to main deploys: schema changes stay additive and are called out for the owner in the finish report.' Decide separately whether production should need a manual promotion once design partners use it.

### D208 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** Shared header, p.6: 'Never weaken an existing safety rule, cap or check to make a test pass.'

**Why it is wrong.** Unverifiable as written: nothing in the repository marks which tests and constants are safety checks (the pytest markers are browser and slow only), so neither CI nor a reviewer can see that one was weakened, and the pull-request template asks for an ADR only for 'the risk policy'. The rule also protects less than it seems: the caps are safe, but a pack's own policy may raise automation (rule outcome AUTO, a per-label threshold below the review threshold) with no validation.

### D209 (shipping-baseline)

**The plan says.** The plan has no rule for release versioning or for license headers (A1.4 asks only for LICENSE and NOTICE).

**Why it is wrong.** The first public release (stage 3) will be the first tag ever cut; the version lives in two files with no consistency check, there is no engine changelog, and no source file states its licence. ## Every opportunity recorded

### Per-case prediction files as the unit of evidence (principles)

**Problem.** The harness aggregates and throws away per-case results, so every new statistic, re-ranking or method change means calling paid providers again, and nothing can be recomputed byte-for-byte. Hosted remote evaluations are capped at 200 cases per call.

**Proposal.** Have `evaluate` optionally write a predictions file (case id, truth, predicted label, probabilities, outcome, answering model; never text), content-hashed and referenced from the report. Compute all intervals, McNemar pairs and ranks from these files. A grade then becomes: pack digest + set hash + predictions hash + method version, which is what gets signed. It also lets large sets be run in resumable chunks under the 200-case cap and fits the owner's low-spend rule.

- src/mendari/evals/harness.py:104-108 - results are passed to build_report and dropped
- src/mendari/server/app.py:259 - REMOTE_EVAL_LIMIT = 200
- $ python det.py -> metrics are already deterministic given the same predictions (all five benchmarks reproduce)

### Record the model version that actually answered, everywhere (principles)

**Problem.** Jev already stamps the answering model on each answer; the LLM provider learns it from the response but records the requested alias, and reports and leaderboard rows carry only the configured id. Aliases such as anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 can change underneath a published number.

**Proposal.** Have the LLM provider stamp the answering model on its answers as Jev does, and add `providers[slot].effective_models` (a set) to the evaluation report and the leaderboard row. Mark a row stale when the effective version differs from the one graded: this gives A9's 're-run when a provider reports a new model version' a trigger for free. Then delete or use `ProviderOutput.extra`.

- src/mendari/providers/llm.py:202-204 - effective_model goes only into `extra`
- $ git grep -n -w extra -- src python -> no reader; src/mendari/evals/harness.py:202-205 - the report uses decision.provider_info

### Derive the four arms from the manifest instead of hand-listing runs (principles)

**Problem.** Arms exist only as a convention in how someone typed `--run`; the fourth arm is absent everywhere and four of five leaderboards have drifted to older pack versions.

**Proposal.** A small function that walks a variant tree and returns the set of remote provider types gives the arm of any configuration (none, {jev}, {llm}, {jev, llm}); exactly that classified the 166 committed rows in this audit. `mendari scoreboard <pack>` can then enumerate every variant combination, group by arm, and refuse to write rows for any digest but the current one. Add an `any_of` of rules, jev and llm to each safety slot so arm 4 exists and is the safest-by-construction configuration.

### Make 'synthetic only' checkable with the tag the sandbox already writes (principles)

**Problem.** The synthetic-only rule is a sentence on screen. The sandbox already tags every generated FHIR resource with a dedicated code, but nothing checks for it.

**Proposal.** Add a deployment data policy (`synthetic` or `phi`). In `synthetic` mode the FHIR and CDS Hooks entry points refuse resources without the sandbox tag, Try it requires the acknowledgement, and the badge reads from the policy; in `phi` mode the badge changes and PHI mode `off` is refused at startup. This is deterministic, needs no detector, and removes the false 'synthetic data only' badge from real deployments.

### Default install with no copyleft dependency (licensing)

**Problem.** psycopg, psycopg-binary and psycopg-pool (LGPL-3.0-only) are required for every install, including SQLite-only self-hosters, and are the only copyleft packages in the 34-package runtime closure. Some open-source review processes treat LGPL as a stop even though importing it is compatible.

**Proposal.** Move them to an optional `postgres` extra with a clear error when the extra is missing. The imports are already lazy inside the Postgres backend. The Dockerfile, deploy templates and the Vercel build (which installs from pyproject.toml) must install the extra, so this needs a proven hosted build before it merges; if that proof is hard, keep the dependency and document LGPL compliance instead.

**Problem.** A pack's licence is an unchecked string and nothing declares which third-party code systems its logic and data contain. **Proposal.** Validate `license` as an SPDX expression; add a manifest field listing the code systems a pack embeds; have the pack check detect known proprietary systems (the AMA CPT URL, X12, SNOMED CT) in logic, mapping and data and require the declaration; show 'contains CPT: AMA licence required at your site' on the Decision Card and Hub. ### One gated, attested release pipeline (A1)

**Problem.** PyPI and image publishing are two independent workflows on the same tag. Images skip the test run and the tag/version check, the engine image is pushed untested at tag time, no check ties a tag to main, and nothing ties an image a health system receives back to a reviewed commit.

**Proposal.** Fold image publishing into release.yml behind the tested build; smoke-test every image; refuse a tag whose commit is not on main; add build-provenance attestations and an SBOM for each image and sign the images (the PyPI action, to my recollection, already attests the wheel under trusted publishing). **Problem.** Mode off writes the input into the record whose digest is chained, which is the single reason plaintext 'can't be erased'. It forces a special guard, a legacy-data problem and a purge that silently does nothing.

**Proposal.** Store the input and evidence in the side table in all three modes (plain in off, sealed in encrypt, absent in hash). Purge, erase and retention then behave identically everywhere, the A5.1b guard shrinks to 'unencrypted only in open local mode', and no future deployment can create unerasable patient text.

### Open inputs on demand instead of on every list load (A5)

**Problem.** GET /api/review decrypts every pending decision in the page (up to 500) and chains one input.read per decision on each request, and /api/feedback does the same. The chain fills with reads that say nothing about who actually looked at which case, and reviewers are shown more patient text than they need.

**Proposal.** Return the queue sealed and open one decision's input when the reviewer opens its drawer. Each input.read then means a person looked at that case, which is what a health system's privacy office will ask the access log to show.

### Per-organization data keys (A5)

**Problem.** One global PHI key seals every organization's inputs, and the associated data binds a ciphertext to its decision but not to its organization. Rotation means re-encrypting every row, and an organization that leaves cannot have its data made unreadable on its own.

**Proposal.** Envelope encryption: a data key per organization, wrapped by the deployment key. Rotation becomes re-wrapping a handful of keys, and off-boarding an organization is deleting its key. This fits A6 (organizations) and gives design partners a concrete isolation claim.

### A public, verifiable registry log with a Mendari counter-signature (A10)

**Problem.** Trust in a pulled pack rests on a key the same registry lists, pinned on first use, with no revocation and no record of who published or withdrew what.

**Proposal.** Give the registry a signing key whose public half ships in the client, counter-sign every accepted version and every yank, and expose the hash-chained event log read-only so anyone can verify it. It reuses the engine's chain design and the existing Ed25519 code, removes trust-on-first-use, makes yanks provable, and gives A9's 'signed, immutable results' a home.

**Problem.** Every search, health check, namespace answer and Hub home view loads every version's full metadata, card and leaderboard included, and a card has no size limit. ### Hermetic and faster local test loop (shipping-baseline)

**Problem.** A local default run takes about 200 seconds, skips 270 Postgres tests without saying it differs from CI, and creates var/mendari.db in the working directory during collection.

**Proposal.** Build the Vercel app lazily so importing mendari.server.vercel has no side effects; print a one-line summary when Postgres variants are skipped; add pytest-xdist (each test already has its own tmp_path and its own Postgres schema) and a marked fast lane for the pure-logic files, which ran 167 tests in 9 seconds here.

### One notice, rendered everywhere a clinician can see a decision (shipping-baseline)

**Problem.** The surfaces most likely to reach a clinician (CDS Hooks cards, the SMART patient view, Decision Cards) carry no research-preview or not-a-device wording, while developer pages do.

**Proposal.** Put the notice in the decision itself: a `notice` field in DecisionResult.to_dict, a note on the FHIR GuidanceResponse and Task, the CDS card's detail, and the Decision Card header, all from one constant, with pack-level additions (for example the inbox pack's 911 text) declared in pack.yaml and shown wherever that pack decides.

### Provenance for the hand-written evaluation sets (shipping-baseline)

**Problem.** The sets that matter most for safety claims (emergency paraphrases, exclusions, urgent referrals, unsafe drafts and their holdouts: 290 records) are hand-written files with a one-line comment as their only record. Nothing says who wrote them, when, whether the holdout was really written before tuning, or checks them for identifiers.

**Proposal.** Add a provenance block per dataset in pack.yaml (author, date, method, tuning or holdout, frozen at which pack version) that the card prints, plus a CI identifier screen over dataset text. This is a small first step of A8's evaluation-set builder and makes the 'never used for tuning' claim auditable from git history.
